question: Why is it important for nurses to talk directly with teenagers during nutrition counselling, rather than only talking to their parents?

options.A: It legally removes parental responsibility for food purchases.
options.B: Teenagers refuse to speak to adults unless parents leave the room.
options.C: It helps teens build personal responsibility for making healthy choices.
options.D: Parents have no influence over what teenagers buy or eat.

explanation: Brilliant thinking! When teens are involved in the conversation, they feel respected and are more likely to actually stick to healthy habits. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T007#GNS227_U2_T007_h7)

question: A nurse is talking to an overweight teenager about healthy eating. What is the most encouraging and effective approach?

options.A: Directly warning the teenager about how bad their body shape looks
options.B: Focusing the discussion on energy, athletic performance, and well-being without shaming
options.C: Ignoring diet completely and focusing only on prescription medication
options.D: Strictly forbidding all favorite foods to force rapid weight loss

explanation: Encouragement wins every time! Focusing on feeling good, having more energy, and performing well works much better than shaming or strict starvation diets. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T007#GNS227_U2_T007_h7)

question: By about what percentage does a pregnant woman's blood volume increase?

options.A: Up to twenty percent
options.B: Up to fifty percent
options.C: Up to ten percent
options.D: Up to seventy-five percent

explanation: You've got this! A mum's blood volume shoots up by nearly half (50%) to carry enough oxygen and nutrients to her growing baby and placenta. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T008#GNS227_U2_T008_h1)

question: Why does a pregnant woman's body absorb nutrients much better?

options.A: To slow down the overall digestion process in the stomach
options.B: To support the higher metabolic demands of the mother and fetus
options.C: To decrease the total amount of food the mother needs to consume
options.D: To prevent the mother from gaining any excess body weight

explanation: Great thinking! Her body works smarter to feed both her own tissues and the baby without running completely out of nutrients. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T008#GNS227_U2_T008_h1)

question: About how many extra calories a day are needed in the later stages of pregnancy?

options.A: Three hundred calories
options.B: Two thousand calories
options.C: One thousand calories
options.D: Fifty calories

explanation: Spot on! An extra 300 calories a day—like a small, nourishing snack—is usually all it takes to fuel the final trimesters. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T008#GNS227_U2_T008_h2)

question: What is the main job of extra protein during pregnancy?

options.A: Regulating sudden shifts in blood pressure
options.B: Preventing common digestive discomforts
options.C: Building uterine, breast, and fetal tissues
options.D: Providing quick energy for the mother's brain

explanation: Nailed it! Protein acts like the primary building blocks for the baby's growth, plus the mum's changing uterus and breasts. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T008#GNS227_U2_T008_h2)

question: Why is folic acid so important before and during early pregnancy?

options.A: To prevent neural tube defects
options.B: To strengthen the mother's bones
options.C: To lower maternal blood pressure
options.D: To stop excessive morning sickness

explanation: Brilliant! Folic acid is a true lifesaver in early pregnancy, helping the baby's brain and spine form properly. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T008#GNS227_U2_T008_h3)

question: A mum at 20 weeks is feeling very tired and has low hemoglobin. What supplement should she likely get more of?

options.A: Stop all calcium tablets
options.B: Eliminate dietary proteins
options.C: Reduce daily fluid intake
options.D: Increase iron intake

explanation: You got it! That tired feeling and low hemoglobin scream iron deficiency anemia, which is super common when blood volume expands. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T008#GNS227_U2_T008_h3)

question: Severe dehydration in a pregnant patient can trigger which scary complication?

options.A: High blood glucose levels
options.B: Excessive bone hardening
options.C: Premature contractions
options.D: Rapid fetal hair growth

explanation: Exactly! When a mum is short on water, her blood volume drops, and her uterus can get irritated and start contracting too early. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T008#GNS227_U2_T008_h4)

question: Why does not drinking enough water put pregnant women at higher risk for urinary tract infections (UTIs)?

options.A: Faster bacterial growth caused by extra dietary fat
options.B: Reduced flushing of bacteria from the urinary tract
options.C: Increased production of sugary urine by the kidneys
options.D: Lower body temperature slowing down immune cells

explanation: Makes total sense, right? Drinking plenty of water means regular peeing, which naturally washes away nasty bacteria before they cause trouble. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T008#GNS227_U2_T008_h4)

question: Sudden, heavy weight gain in the second half of pregnancy usually points to what?

options.A: Rapid increase in maternal muscle mass
options.B: Normal development of twin fetuses
options.C: Fluid retention or gestational hypertension
options.D: Excellent absorption of dietary protein

explanation: Spot on! If the scale jumps suddenly along with swelling, it's a red flag for water retention or high blood pressure issues. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T008#GNS227_U2_T008_h5)

question: When planning meals for a pregnant patient in your community, what should guide you the most?

options.A: Focusing exclusively on raw vegetable diets
options.B: Using only expensive imported vitamin supplements
options.C: Eliminating all traditional family recipes
options.D: Local food availability and household finances

explanation: You nailed clinical reality! Advice is useless if the family can't afford it or find the ingredients nearby. Always keep it practical! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T008#GNS227_U2_T008_h5)

question: What is a great trick to help a mum manage early morning pregnancy nausea?

options.A: Remaining completely fasting until the afternoon hours
options.B: Eating small, dry carbohydrate snacks before getting out of bed
options.C: Consuming a heavy, high-fat breakfast right away
options.D: Drinking a large cup of cold whole milk immediately upon waking

explanation: Such a classic nursing tip! A dry biscuit before standing up keeps blood sugar stable and calms that empty, nauseous tummy. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T008#GNS227_U2_T008_h6)

question: Why do pregnant women struggle so often with constipation?

options.A: Progesterone slows down normal bowel motility
options.B: Maternal kidneys absorb all water from the stool
options.C: The growing baby physically blocks the stomach
options.D: High protein diets stop intestinal movement

explanation: You got it! Pregnancy hormones relax smooth muscles all over the body, which unfortunately puts the brakes on digestion too. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T008#GNS227_U2_T008_h6)

question: A patient's mother-in-law says she shouldn't eat eggs or the baby will be born hairless. How should you, as the nurse, respond?

options.A: Agree with the cultural belief to avoid causing family tension
options.B: Tell the patient to ignore her family completely and eat in secret
options.C: Prescribe an expensive chemical supplement to replace the eggs
options.D: Respectfully explain that eggs are a safe, rich source of protein and essential nutrients

explanation: Well done! Always respect family and culture, but gently guide patients toward safe, nutritious truths without sounding rude. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T008#GNS227_U2_T008_h7)

question: When counseling pregnant women about traditional food habits, which approach is NOT helpful?

options.A: Listening carefully to the patient's family and cultural beliefs
options.B: Incorporating affordable local staples like beans and dark leafy greens
options.C: Identifying harmful taboos without disrespecting the community
options.D: Insisting that only imported foreign foods can provide proper prenatal nutrition

explanation: Spot on! Good nursing care relies on affordable, local foods that everyday families can actually get, not expensive foreign items. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T008#GNS227_U2_T008_h7)

question: Which hormone is primarily responsible for triggering the milk ejection or let-down reflex during breastfeeding?

options.A: Estrogen
options.B: Progesterone
options.C: Prolactin
options.D: Oxytocin

explanation: Oxytocin causes the tiny muscles around the milk glands to squeeze, pushing the milk down the ducts so the baby can drink it easily. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T009#GNS227_U2_T009_h1)

question: What happens to a mother's body stores if her diet lacks certain essential nutrients while she is breastfeeding?

options.A: The chemical composition of her milk changes to match her poor diet
options.B: Her baby stops growing immediately due to a sudden lack of calories
options.C: Her body draws from its own tissue stores to keep the milk nutritious
options.D: Milk production stops completely until her diet improves

explanation: Maternal physiology prioritizes infant nutrition, often depleting maternal reserves like bone calcium if dietary intake is insufficient. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T009#GNS227_U2_T009_h1)

question: Approximately how many extra calories does an exclusively breastfeeding mother need each day?

options.A: 100 to 200 calories
options.B: 450 to 500 calories
options.C: 800 to 1000 calories
options.D: No extra calories are needed

explanation: Making breast milk takes a lot of energy, requiring about 450 to 500 extra calories daily for an exclusively nursing mother. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T009#GNS227_U2_T009_h2)

question: A nursing mother complains of extreme fatigue and a noticeable drop in milk supply after starting a very strict, low-calorie weight loss diet. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Inadequate daily caloric intake to support milk synthesis
options.B: A sudden hormonal imbalance unrelated to her food intake
options.C: Normal physiological changes that happen at three months postpartum
options.D: Drinking too much plain water instead of sugary beverages

explanation: Drastic calorie restriction robs the body of the energy required to make milk, leading to fatigue and reduced supply. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T009#GNS227_U2_T009_h2)

question: Why are omega-3 fatty acids particularly important in the diet of a breastfeeding mother?

options.A: They support the infant's brain and nervous system development
options.B: They stimulate the immediate release of oxytocin during feeding
options.C: They act as the primary source of daily energy for the mother
options.D: They prevent the mother from gaining too much postpartum weight

explanation: Omega-3 fatty acids, especially DHA passed through breast milk, play a major role in building the baby's brain and eyes. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T009#GNS227_U2_T009_h3)

question: What is the primary role of increased protein intake during the lactation period?

options.A: To provide quick energy during night feedings
options.B: To support tissue repair and milk synthesis
options.C: To maintain hydration and fluid balance
options.D: To prevent the baby from developing infant colic

explanation: Proteins supply the building blocks needed to create milk and help the mother's body heal from childbirth. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T009#GNS227_U2_T009_h3)

question: What happens to maternal bones if a breastfeeding mother does not consume enough calcium in her diet?

options.A: Her bones become significantly denser and stronger
options.B: Calcium is drawn from her bones to maintain milk quality
options.C: Her body stops producing milk until she takes supplements
options.D: Her breast milk becomes completely devoid of calcium

explanation: The body will take calcium from the mother's bones to ensure the baby's milk has what it needs if dietary intake falls short. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T009#GNS227_U2_T009_h4)

question: Why is adequate iron intake particularly crucial immediately following childbirth and during lactation?

options.A: To help the infant digest complex carbohydrates in the milk
options.B: To stimulate the mammary glands to produce more milk volume
options.C: To prevent postpartum anemia and recover from blood loss during delivery
options.D: To regulate the mother's blood pressure during night feeds

explanation: Childbirth involves blood loss, and iron helps build new red blood cells to keep the mother strong and energized. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T009#GNS227_U2_T009_h4)

question: Roughly what percentage of breast milk is composed of water?

options.A: 99 percent
options.B: 70 percent
options.C: 88 percent
options.D: 50 percent

explanation: Breast milk is mostly water, which is why keeping hydrated is so important for the nursing mother's fluid balance. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T009#GNS227_U2_T009_h5)

question: What is a good practical habit for a breastfeeding mother to maintain proper hydration throughout the day?

options.A: Drinking at least five liters of water before getting out of bed
options.B: Avoiding all fluids for two hours after every feeding
options.C: Drinking a glass of water every time she sits down to nurse
options.D: Drinking only when she feels severe dizziness or dry mouth

explanation: Nursing triggers thirst, and linking a glass of water to each feeding session is an easy way to stay properly hydrated. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T009#GNS227_U2_T009_h5)

question: Which local Nigerian vegetable is commonly used in soups to provide essential iron and vitamins for nursing mothers?

options.A: Raw cocoa powder
options.B: Refined white sugar
options.C: Ugu (fluted pumpkin leaves)
options.D: Dried cassava flakes

explanation: Ugu leaves are rich in iron and vital vitamins, making them a staple in local postpartum soups across Nigeria. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T009#GNS227_U2_T009_h6)

question: A nursing mother in a local clinic asks for an affordable, traditional Nigerian food option that provides both fluid and easy energy during early morning hours. What is a suitable recommendation?

options.A: Raw bitter kola chewed without any water
options.B: A carbonated sugary soft drink with dry biscuits
options.C: Warm pap (akamu) prepared with milk and groundnuts
options.D: Heavy dry gin infused with local roots

explanation: Pap is a traditional, easily digestible meal that provides fluid, warmth, and steady energy when enriched with milk and groundnuts. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T009#GNS227_U2_T009_h6)

question: What is a common effect on an infant if a breastfeeding mother consumes excessive amounts of caffeine?

options.A: Severe weight gain and fluid retention
options.B: Jitteriness and sleep disturbances
options.C: Uncontrolled drowsiness and deep coma
options.D: Immediate development of infant jaundice

explanation: Babies process caffeine very slowly, so too much of it from breast milk can make them restless and unable to sleep. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T009#GNS227_U2_T009_h7)

question: Which of the following practices regarding alcohol is safest for a nursing mother?

options.A: Consuming alcohol immediately before every single nursing session to relax the baby
options.B: Mixing alcohol directly into infant formula to help the baby sleep through the night
options.C: Drinking large amounts of beer daily because it is traditionally believed to boost milk supply
options.D: Avoiding heavy or frequent drinking and waiting several hours after a drink before nursing

explanation: Alcohol enters breast milk quickly, so minimizing intake and allowing time for the body to clear it protects the infant. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T009#GNS227_U2_T009_h7)

question: What is the most effective approach a nurse should take when providing nutritional counseling to a nursing mother?

options.A: Assess her current diet and suggest affordable, local food options
options.B: Demand that she buy expensive imported supplements and vitamins
options.C: Provide a rigid meal plan without asking about her cultural preferences
options.D: Assume she already knows everything because postpartum nutrition is instinctive

explanation: Good counseling respects the mother's financial and cultural reality by building on affordable, local food sources she already knows. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T009#GNS227_U2_T009_h8)

question: Which of the following is considered a classic sign of maternal depletion that a nurse should watch out for?

options.A: Chronic fatigue and hair loss
options.B: Rapid thickening of tooth enamel
options.C: Decreased need for hours of sleep
options.D: Sudden increase in physical stamina

explanation: When a mother's nutritional stores run low to support milk production, she may experience exhaustion, hair thinning, and fatigue. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T009#GNS227_U2_T009_h8)

question: Which life stage has the fastest human growth rate, coming in second right after infancy?

options.A: Adolescence
options.B: Toddlerhood
options.C: Young adulthood
options.D: Middle childhood

explanation: You've got this! Adolescence is well known as the second fastest period of human growth, right behind infancy. Your body is doing amazing things during these teenage years! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T010#GNS227_U2_T010_h1)

question: Why is good nutrition during the teenage years so crucial for adolescent girls?

options.A: It completely prevents common childhood infections
options.B: It prepares their bodies for future reproductive health and strong bones
options.C: It permanently stops all future height increases
options.D: It eliminates the need for any diet changes later in life

explanation: Great job! Eating well during your teen years directly builds your skeletal structure and gets your body ready for future health and motherhood. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T010#GNS227_U2_T010_h1)

question: What natural monthly bodily change affects an adolescent girl's need for extra iron?

options.A: Ovulation
options.B: Menarche
options.C: The growth spurt
options.D: Pubarche

explanation: Spot on! Menarche (the start of monthly periods) means the body needs to replenish its iron stores regularly. You're doing great! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T010#GNS227_U2_T010_h2)

question: A 14-year-old girl is growing fast and has started her monthly periods. How does this affect her food and nutrient needs?

options.A: She only needs extra water and no other dietary changes
options.B: Her nutritional demands decrease because her body is slowing down
options.C: Her nutritional demands remain exactly the same as childhood
options.D: Her nutritional demands increase significantly to support growth and blood loss

explanation: Exactly! Rapid body growth plus monthly blood loss means she needs more energy, protein, and key minerals to stay strong and healthy. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T010#GNS227_U2_T010_h2)

question: Why do teenage girls need more daily iron in their diet than younger children do?

options.A: To prevent soft bones from a lack of sunlight
options.B: To support monthly period blood loss and growing muscles
options.C: To maintain normal skin color and elasticity
options.D: To help digest heavy local meals easily

explanation: You nailed it! Monthly periods and rapid physical growth use up iron quickly, so eating more iron-rich foods helps prevent anemia. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T010#GNS227_U2_T010_h3)

question: What is the main long-term risk of not getting enough calcium while you are a teenager?

options.A: Chronic tiredness and sudden muscle weakness
options.B: Lower bone strength and higher risk of weak bones in old age
options.C: Delayed puberty and slow height growth
options.D: Severe vitamin deficiency like rickets

explanation: That's right! Your teenage years are your main window to build strong bones. Missing calcium now can lead to easily broken bones when you're older. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T010#GNS227_U2_T010_h3)

question: What type of food should make up the biggest part of an adolescent girl's daily energy intake?

options.A: Refined table sugars
options.B: Pure protein powders
options.C: Saturated animal fats
options.D: Complex carbohydrates

explanation: Wonderful! Complex carbs (like yam, brown rice, and beans) give growing teens steady, lasting energy and healthy fiber. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T010#GNS227_U2_T010_h4)

question: Why is cutting all fats out of a teenage girl's diet a bad idea?

options.A: It causes an instant drop in body temperature
options.B: It guarantees severe muscle wasting in the arms and legs
options.C: It stops all physical growth and shrinks bones
options.D: It can mess up normal hormone balance and block key vitamin absorption

explanation: Spot on! Healthy fats are super important for making hormones and helping your body soak up vitamins like A, D, E, and K. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T010#GNS227_U2_T010_h4)

question: What is the most common nutritional problem facing adolescent girls in Nigeria today?

options.A: Pellagra from maize diets
options.B: Beriberi from polished rice
options.C: Iron-deficiency anemia
options.D: Scurvy from lack of citrus fruits

explanation: You got it! Iron-deficiency anemia is the top nutritional challenge for Nigerian teenage girls due to diet and monthly blood loss. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T010#GNS227_U2_T010_h5)

question: What do we mean by the term 'hidden hunger' in teenage nutrition?

options.A: Eating enough calories to feel full, but missing vital vitamins and minerals
options.B: An eating disorder where teenagers hide food
options.C: Feeling constantly starved despite eating three big meals
options.D: An inability to feel full after eating fiber

explanation: Brilliant! Hidden hunger happens when your belly feels full, but your body is still starving for the micronutrients it needs to thrive. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T010#GNS227_U2_T010_h5)

question: Which of these is a common cultural barrier to good nutrition for some Nigerian teenage girls?

options.A: A total lack of local markets selling staple foods
options.B: Cultural food taboos that save protein-rich foods for adult males
options.C: Mandatory government laws banning green vegetables
options.D: Traditional ceremonies forcing teens to fast for whole months

explanation: True! Some traditional practices mistakenly keep young girls from eating nourishing foods like eggs, meat, or fish. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T010#GNS227_U2_T010_h6)

question: How does eating a lot of cheap fast food affect a teenage girl's nutrition?

options.A: It completely stops iron-deficiency anemia
options.B: It gives empty calories while pushing aside healthy traditional foods
options.C: It supplies all necessary iron and calcium for bone growth
options.D: It improves vitamin absorption in the gut

explanation: You're doing great! Fast foods are packed with fats and sugars but lack real nutrients, often replacing healthier home-cooked meals. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T010#GNS227_U2_T010_h6)

question: What physical sign in the inner eyelids or nail beds is a classic warning sign of possible anemia?

options.A: Erythema
options.B: Jaundice
options.C: Pallor
options.D: Cyanosis

explanation: Spot on! Pale (pallor) inner eyelids and nail beds tell us hemoglobin levels might be low, which is a classic sign of anemia. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T010#GNS227_U2_T010_h7)

question: A nurse is checking a 15-year-old girl who feels very tired, dizzy, and has pale nail beds. What is the best first step to take?

options.A: Test her for color blindness
options.B: Order an immediate full-body MRI scan
options.C: Do a mandatory neurological reflex exam
options.D: Check her BMI growth chart and ask what she usually eats

explanation: You got it! Growth charts and a simple diet history help nurses quickly spot physical growth patterns and nutritional gaps causing that fatigue. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T010#GNS227_U2_T010_h7)

question: What is the best way to give nutrition advice to teenage girls in a local community?

options.A: Tell them to stop eating all local carbohydrates right away
options.B: Insist they buy expensive imported vitamin pills from the pharmacy
options.C: Hand them strict foreign meal plans they can't find in local markets
options.D: Recommend affordable local foods that fit their culture and daily life

explanation: Wonderful! Advice works best when it uses cheap, familiar local ingredients that families can easily find, afford, and cook. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T010#GNS227_U2_T010_h8)

question: A nurse wants to help secondary school girls prevent anemia using local foods. Which tip is the most practical?

options.A: Drink lots of black tea right after every big meal
options.B: Eat sugary snacks between classes for quick energy
options.C: Eat local dark greens, beans, and vitamin C-rich fruits
options.D: Avoid all animal protein and fish products

explanation: Spot on! Local greens and beans give iron, and adding vitamin C (like a squeeze of orange or lemon) helps the body absorb that iron much better! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T010#GNS227_U2_T010_h8)

question: Why do women of reproductive age have unique nutritional needs?

options.A: The permanent cessation of bone growth
options.B: Hormonal shifts and potential childbearing
options.C: A natural decrease in physical activity
options.D: Reduced metabolic needs after puberty

explanation: You've got this! Things like monthly periods, pregnancy, and breastfeeding put special demands on a woman's body, meaning she needs the right nutrients to stay strong and healthy. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T011#GNS227_U2_T011_h1)

question: Why is eating a balanced diet so important for women during their reproductive years?

options.A: It prepares the body for potential pregnancy and protects long-term health
options.B: It guarantees an increase in overall daily muscle mass
options.C: It eliminates the need for any future dietary supplements
options.D: It completely stops the symptoms of premenstrual syndrome

explanation: Great thinking! Keeping good nutrient stores ready helps support a healthy body now and protects both mom and baby if pregnancy happens down the line. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T011#GNS227_U2_T011_h1)

question: What is the main job of carbohydrates in our daily diet?

options.A: Transporting fat-soluble vitamins through blood
options.B: Providing primary fuel for the brain and muscles
options.C: Building strong structural bone matrix
options.D: Synthesizing steroid reproductive hormones

explanation: Spot on! Carbs break down into glucose, which is your body's favorite energy source to keep you moving and studying all day long. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T011#GNS227_U2_T011_h2)

question: Why are healthy fats especially important for women's reproductive health?

options.A: They support proper hormone synthesis and cellular health
options.B: They completely prevent iron-deficiency anemia during menses
options.C: They replace the need for dietary protein intake
options.D: They act as the main source of immediate energy for sprinting

explanation: Well done! Fats act as building blocks for reproductive hormones and also help your body soak up vital vitamins. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T011#GNS227_U2_T011_h2)

question: Why is getting enough folate so crucial for women of reproductive age?

options.A: It maintains bone density in the lower spine
options.B: It stops heavy bleeding during the menstrual cycle
options.C: It directly increases daily red blood cell counts
options.D: It prevents neural tube defects in early pregnancy

explanation: Exactly right! Folate helps cells divide rapidly and protects the baby's developing spine and brain during the very early weeks of pregnancy. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T011#GNS227_U2_T011_h3)

question: Which food source gives us iron that our bodies can absorb the easiest?

options.A: Inorganic iron found in mineral spring water
options.B: Heme iron found in animal products
options.C: Non-heme iron found in leafy green vegetables
options.D: Fortified iron found in refined white flour

explanation: You got it! Heme iron from meats, fish, and poultry is easily taken up by your body compared to plant sources. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T011#GNS227_U2_T011_h3)

question: How can being significantly underweight or overweight affect a woman's reproductive system?

options.A: They can disrupt ovulation and menstrual regularity
options.B: They completely eliminate the need for dietary iron
options.C: They permanently increase overall daily energy expenditure
options.D: They accelerate the onset of natural menopause

explanation: That's correct! Our bodies need a healthy balance of energy and body fat to signal hormones properly and keep cycles regular. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T011#GNS227_U2_T011_h4)

question: A client comes to you asking for advice on diet and irregular ovulation. What is the best starting point?

options.A: Focus on whole foods, healthy weight management, and essential micronutrients
options.B: Rely entirely on heavy vitamin supplements instead of eating meals
options.C: Drink large amounts of caffeinated coffee to boost resting metabolism
options.D: Eliminate all carbohydrates completely from your daily meals

explanation: Awesome choice! Real, wholesome food and steady weight management give the body the stable foundation it needs for natural hormonal balance. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T011#GNS227_U2_T011_h4)

question: Why is drinking plenty of water especially critical for a nursing mother?

options.A: Lactation permanently increases core body temperature
options.B: Nursing mothers completely stop feeling thirsty
options.C: Milk production requires extra sodium from blood
options.D: Breast milk is composed mostly of water

explanation: Spot on! Since breast milk is mostly water, nursing mums need extra fluids to keep up their milk supply and stay hydrated. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T011#GNS227_U2_T011_h5)

question: Why do a pregnant woman's overall nutrient needs go up so much?

options.A: To make up for a complete shutdown of maternal digestion
options.B: To replace the need for normal maternal fat storage
options.C: To prevent the mother from ever experiencing physical fatigue
options.D: To support fetal growth, placental development, and maternal changes

explanation: You nailed it! Growing a baby and expanding your blood volume takes a lot of extra energy and building blocks from the foods mom eats. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T011#GNS227_U2_T011_h5)

question: What is a common reason for iron-deficiency anemia in communities that rely mostly on plant-based foods?

options.A: Excessive consumption of lean red meat products
options.B: Low bioavailability of non-heme iron in plant foods
options.C: A complete lack of carbohydrates in local markets
options.D: Too much calcium blocking all stomach acid

explanation: Correct! Plant-based iron is harder for our bodies to absorb than iron from meat, making anemia more common if diets aren't carefully planned. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T011#GNS227_U2_T011_h6)

question: As a nurse assessing a patient with severe iron-deficiency anemia, what physical sign are you most likely to spot?

options.A: Pallor of the mucous membranes and nail beds
options.B: Yellow discoloration of the skin and eyes
options.C: Swelling in the hands and lower feet
options.D: Rapid and excessive involuntary weight gain

explanation: Great clinical eye! Low hemoglobin means fewer red blood cells, which makes the inner eyelids, gums, and nail beds look pale. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T011#GNS227_U2_T011_h6)

question: Why should a nurse always recommend locally available and affordable foods when giving diet advice?

options.A: It ensures the client can maintain the diet long-term
options.B: It guarantees that the food contains zero calories
options.C: It replaces the need for any professional medical care
options.D: It prevents the client from ever needing clean water

explanation: You got it! Good advice has to be practical. If people can't find or afford the food nearby, they won't be able to keep up with the diet. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T011#GNS227_U2_T011_h7)

question: You are counseling a young woman who wants to eat healthier on a tight budget. What is your best approach?

options.A: Suggesting affordable, nutrient-dense local foods that fit her lifestyle
options.B: Handing her an expensive list of imported specialty supplements
options.C: Telling her to eat only raw vegetables for every meal
options.D: Advising her to skip meals until she can afford gourmet foods

explanation: Wonderful nursing care! Always meet your patients where they are with realistic, budget-friendly choices that fit their daily lives. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T011#GNS227_U2_T011_h7)

question: What happens to a mother's body when her diet lacks proper nutrition during pregnancy?

options.A: Maternal blood volume increases beyond normal limits
options.B: The fetus draws nutrients from the mother's own body stores
options.C: Fetal growth remains completely unaffected by maternal diet
options.D: The placenta stops growing completely to save energy

explanation: When food intake is low, the clever baby takes what it needs from your own body reserves! This is why mums can feel so drained. You're doing great learning how the body adapts. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T012#GNS227_U2_T012_h1)

question: Why is the old saying 'eating for two' a bit misleading for expectant mothers?

options.A: It suggests that pregnant women need fewer calories than non-pregnant women
options.B: It encourages doubling food quantity rather than focusing on nutrient quality
options.C: It means the baby eats solid food while still inside the womb
options.D: It applies only to the final month of the pregnancy period

explanation: It's not about eating twice as much food! It's about making smarter, nutrient-packed food choices so both you and baby get the right vitamins. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T012#GNS227_U2_T012_h1)

question: During which stages of pregnancy do women usually need an extra 340 to 450 calories every day?

options.A: The first two weeks after conception
options.B: First trimester only
options.C: During labor and delivery
options.D: Second and third trimesters

explanation: As that little baby starts growing super fast in the later months, the mother needs a small energy boost of extra daily calories! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T012#GNS227_U2_T012_h2)

question: A pregnant mum asks why she needs to eat protein foods like beans and fish. What is the best way to explain this?

options.A: They provide extra sugar to keep your energy levels very high
options.B: They supply protein which helps build the placenta and baby's tissues
options.C: They prevent morning sickness by soothing your stomach lining
options.D: They replace the need for taking any blood-building vitamins

explanation: Protein is like the building blocks for construction! It helps build the baby's muscles, organs, and the placenta too. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T012#GNS227_U2_T012_h2)

question: Why are pregnant mums strongly advised to take folic acid supplements early on?

options.A: To cure severe morning sickness and persistent vomiting
options.B: To help the mother gain weight quickly in the first month
options.C: To lower the risk of developing gestational diabetes later
options.D: To prevent neural tube defects in the baby's brain and spine

explanation: Folic acid is a true protector! It helps form the baby's early brain and spinal cord properly right at the start. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T012#GNS227_U2_T012_h3)

question: Why do healthcare workers often suggest taking citrus fruits or tomatoes along with iron-rich foods?

options.A: Citrus fruits stop the common side effect of constipation
options.B: It prevents the iron supplement from dissolving too fast
options.C: Acidic foods completely remove the metallic taste of iron
options.D: Vitamin C helps the body absorb iron much better

explanation: Vitamin C acts like a friendly helper—it teams up with iron so your tummy can absorb it easily and keep your blood strong! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T012#GNS227_U2_T012_h3)

question: Which of these substances should a pregnant woman completely avoid to keep her baby safe?

options.A: Cows milk
options.B: Alcohol
options.C: Local fish
options.D: Green vegetables

explanation: No amount of alcohol is safe during pregnancy. Steering clear of it protects the baby's healthy development completely. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T012#GNS227_U2_T012_h4)

question: Why must pregnant women avoid eating raw or undercooked meats?

options.A: Raw meat causes severe allergic skin rashes in expectant mothers
options.B: Because cooked meat has more protein than raw meat
options.C: To prevent dangerous foodborne infections that can harm the pregnancy
options.D: Undercooked meat takes much longer for the stomach to digest

explanation: Raw meat can hide tricky germs and parasites like toxoplasma. Cooking food thoroughly keeps both mum and baby safe from infections! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T012#GNS227_U2_T012_h4)

question: A pregnant patient is struggling with morning sickness and finds it hard to eat three big meals. What is the best advice?

options.A: Force yourself to eat large plates of heavy food to keep your strength up
options.B: Eat small, frequent snacks throughout the day to keep something in the stomach
options.C: Drink strong coffee on an empty stomach to wake up your digestive tract
options.D: Stop drinking all fluids completely until the vomiting stops entirely

explanation: An empty stomach can actually make nausea worse! Nibbling on small, light snacks often helps keep the tummy settled. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T012#GNS227_U2_T012_h5)

question: What is the main reason why many pregnant women experience constipation?

options.A: Drinking water causes the bowels to become blocked
options.B: Prenatal vitamins stop the liver from producing bile
options.C: High levels of progesterone slow down movement through the digestive tract
options.D: The baby takes up all the space in the stomach and intestines

explanation: Pregnancy hormones relax the body's muscles, including the gut. This means digestion slows down a bit, which is totally normal! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T012#GNS227_U2_T012_h5)

question: Why is it wonderful for Nigerian nurses to recommend local soups like ugwu and egusi during nutrition talks?

options.A: They are affordable, culturally familiar, and rich in essential nutrients
options.B: They are the only foods allowed by traditional customs during pregnancy
options.C: They replace the need for antenatal clinic attendance
options.D: They completely eliminate the risk of gestational high blood pressure

explanation: Our local soups are packed with vitamins, iron, and good fats! They are easy to find, pocket-friendly, and nourishing. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T012#GNS227_U2_T012_h6)

question: A mum says she cannot afford expensive imported foods sometimes shown in diet books. What is your best response?

options.A: Tell her to borrow money so she can buy foreign foods from the supermarket
options.B: Advise her to skip meals until she can afford the expensive recommended items
options.C: Show her how to combine local staples like beans, local fish, and green vegetables for good nutrition
options.D: Explain that diet does not matter as long as she takes her routine clinic drugs

explanation: You don't need fancy imported foods for a healthy pregnancy! Local foods like beans, fish, and greens give all the power nutrition needed. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T012#GNS227_U2_T012_h6)

question: What is pica, a condition nurses watch out for during dietary checks?

options.A: An allergic reaction to eating citrus fruits during pregnancy
options.B: An excessive thirst that leads to drinking too much water daily
options.C: A complete loss of appetite caused by severe hormonal changes
options.D: A strong craving to eat non-food items like clay, starch, or ice

explanation: Pica happens when a mum craves non-food items like chalk or clay. It's usually the body's way of whispering that she lacks certain minerals like iron! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T012#GNS227_U2_T012_h7)

question: During an antenatal visit, how can a nurse best check a pregnant woman's nutritional status?

options.A: Give her a printed diet sheet in English without asking about her background
options.B: Ask open-ended questions about her usual daily meals and check her weight trend
options.C: Assume she eats well because she looks healthy on the outside
options.D: Wait until after delivery to discuss what kind of food she ate at home

explanation: Chatting warmly about what she actually eats daily and watching her weight trends helps you spot any nutritional gaps early and support her. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T012#GNS227_U2_T012_h7)

question: If a nursing mother's diet lacks enough nutrients, how does her body manage to produce breast milk?

options.A: The body absorbs extra nutrients directly from the air
options.B: Milk production stops completely until diet improves
options.C: The body draws from maternal stores to maintain milk
options.D: Breast milk loses all its essential nutrients instantly

explanation: Nature makes sure the baby gets what it needs! If diet falls short, the mother's body will use its own stored nutrients to keep the milk flowing. Great job understanding maternal priority! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T013#GNS227_U2_T013_h1)

question: Why does breastfeeding usually demand more energy and nutrition from a mother than pregnancy did?

options.A: Continuous milk synthesis requires daily energy and nutrient output
options.B: Mothers lose vital organs temporarily during the birth process
options.C: The infant grows much faster outside the womb than inside
options.D: Digestive efficiency drops significantly after childbirth occurs

explanation: Producing milk every single day is hard work for the body. It takes a steady, high daily supply of calories and nutrients to keep up with the growing baby! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T013#GNS227_U2_T013_h1)

question: Roughly how many extra calories per day does producing breast milk require on average?

options.A: 100 calories
options.B: 1200 calories
options.C: 50 calories
options.D: 500 calories

explanation: Milk production is metabolically demanding, requiring about 500 extra calories daily for an exclusively breastfeeding mother. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T013#GNS227_U2_T013_h2)

question: What can happen if a breastfeeding mother drastically cuts her calories to lose weight too fast?

options.A: It stops the infant from sleeping
options.B: It can reduce the daily milk supply
options.C: It causes permanent bone density loss
options.D: It changes the baby's blood type

explanation: Crash dieting sends a signal to the body to slow down and conserve energy, which can unfortunately cause your milk supply to drop. Slow and steady wins the race! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T013#GNS227_U2_T013_h2)

question: Which type of nutrient is especially important for the baby's brain and nervous system growth?

options.A: Water
options.B: Fats
options.C: Starch
options.D: Fiber

explanation: Healthy dietary fats are superstars here! They provide essential fatty acids that build brain tissue and support your baby's developing nervous system. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T013#GNS227_U2_T013_h3)

question: A nursing mum wants steady, long-lasting energy for her daily chores. What should you recommend she eat?

options.A: Pure cooking oils taken directly by the spoonful
options.B: Salt-free butter eaten in large morning portions
options.C: Simple refined sugars found in carbonated beverages
options.D: Complex carbohydrates like yams and whole grains

explanation: Complex carbs digest slowly and steadily. Foods like yams and whole grains give you the sustained energy needed to care for a newborn all day long! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T013#GNS227_U2_T013_h3)

question: Why is getting enough calcium so crucial for a breastfeeding mother?

options.A: To prevent the baby from developing infantile jaundice
options.B: To make the breast milk taste sweet to the infant
options.C: To ensure the infant's skin develops normally
options.D: To prevent the depletion of her own bone density

explanation: Calcium constantly flows into breast milk. If a mum's diet is low in calcium, her body will borrow it right out of her own bones to protect the milk. Protect those bones, mummies! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T013#GNS227_U2_T013_h4)

question: Which mineral helps a new mother beat fatigue and rebuild iron stores lost during childbirth?

options.A: Sodium
options.B: Calcium
options.C: Potassium
options.D: Iron

explanation: Iron builds hemoglobin, helping mums recover from delivery blood loss and keeping postpartum fatigue and anemia at bay. You've got this! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T013#GNS227_U2_T013_h4)

question: What is the main problem if a breastfeeding mother becomes severely dehydrated?

options.A: It turns the breast milk bright yellow
options.B: It stops the let-down reflex permanently
options.C: It permanently changes the infant's eye color
options.D: It can decrease breast milk supply

explanation: Since breast milk is mostly water, severe dehydration leaves the body with less fluid to make milk. Remember to keep a water bottle close by! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T013#GNS227_U2_T013_h5)

question: What is the best and simplest guide for a nursing mother on how much fluid to drink?

options.A: Drink fluids whenever she feels thirsty
options.B: Avoid all liquids for two hours after each feeding
options.C: Drink only carbonated soft drinks to stay energized
options.D: Force herself to drink ten liters daily regardless of thirst

explanation: Your body's natural thirst cue is a fantastic guide during lactation. Drinking a glass of water during each nursing session is a wonderful habit to build. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T013#GNS227_U2_T013_h5)

question: What might you notice in an infant if the mother consumes too much caffeine?

options.A: Sudden and permanent hair loss
options.B: Continuous deep sleeping for days
options.C: Irritability and jitteriness
options.D: Rapid whitening of the fingernails

explanation: Caffeine is a stimulant that passes through breast milk in small amounts. Too much can make your little one restless, fussy, and wide awake! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T013#GNS227_U2_T013_h6)

question: Which substance requires a nursing mother to wait patiently until it clears her bloodstream before breastfeeding again?

options.A: Alcohol
options.B: Calcium
options.C: Water
options.D: Garlic

explanation: Alcohol passes straight into breast milk and clears out only as it leaves the mother's bloodstream. Timing and caution are key here! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T013#GNS227_U2_T013_h6)

question: Which common local Nigerian vegetable is packed with iron, calcium, and vitamins for nursing mums?

options.A: Dried white table salt
options.B: Polished white rice
options.C: Fluted pumpkin leaves (ugu)
options.D: Refined wheat flour

explanation: Dark leafy greens like ugu are local nutrition powerhouses! They are packed with the iron and vitamins needed to recover well and boost milk production. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T013#GNS227_U2_T013_h7)

question: A nursing mum in the clinic needs affordable protein options available in local Nigerian markets. What should you suggest?

options.A: Processed canned biscuits
options.B: Imported energy drink powders
options.C: Packaged artificial sweeteners
options.D: Beans, crayfish, and lean fish

explanation: Local proteins like beans, crayfish, and fish are budget-friendly, easily accessible, and provide wonderful amino acids for lactation. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T013#GNS227_U2_T013_h7)

question: When counseling a new mother on her diet, what is an important duty for you as a nurse?

options.A: Forbidding the mother from eating local traditional dishes
options.B: Prescribing strict medical weight-loss medications
options.C: Requiring the mother to purchase expensive foreign supplements
options.D: Debunking harmful food myths that restrict healthy eating

explanation: Many cultural myths try to stop mums from eating nutritious local foods after delivery. As nurses, we gently clear up these misconceptions with kindness and facts! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T013#GNS227_U2_T013_h8)

question: Why is getting family members involved in the dietary care of a breastfeeding mother so helpful?

options.A: Family support helps ensure the mother has time to rest and eat
options.B: Family members decide the exact hour the infant should sleep
options.C: Family members must taste all food before the mother eats it
options.D: Relatives are legally responsible for paying for infant formula

explanation: New mums carry a heavy load! When family helps share chores and cooking, it gives the mother the breathing room she needs to nourish herself properly. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T013#GNS227_U2_T013_h8)

question: What do we call the natural, progressive loss of muscle mass and strength as people grow older?

options.A: Osteoporosis
options.B: Atrophic gastritis
options.C: Cachexia
options.D: Sarcopenia

explanation: You'll often hear this called sarcopenia! It's the age-related drop in muscle mass and function that naturally lowers calorie needs as we age. You've got this! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T014#GNS227_U2_T014_h1)

question: Why does atrophic gastritis often lead to vitamin B12 deficiency in older adults?

options.A: It speeds up the digestion of vitamins before the body can use them
options.B: It reduces stomach acid and intrinsic factor needed for absorption
options.C: It destroys the bacteria in the gut that naturally manufacture B12
options.D: It causes the liver to store less vitamin B12 than normal

explanation: Spot on! When stomach acid and intrinsic factor drop, the body struggles to break B12 away from food and absorb it in the gut. Great nursing insight to keep in mind! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T014#GNS227_U2_T014_h1)

question: Why do older adults need a good amount of protein relative to their body weight?

options.A: To prevent the rapid buildup of visceral fat around internal organs
options.B: To counteract age-related muscle loss and support immune function
options.C: To provide extra calories for increased daily physical activity
options.D: To compensate for faster breakdown of protein in the kidneys

explanation: Exactly! Higher protein helps older adults fight off muscle wasting (sarcopenia) and keeps their immune system strong. Simple and vital! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T014#GNS227_U2_T014_h2)

question: Which type of dietary fiber is especially important to include in the daily meals of older adults?

options.A: Low-residue fiber to completely eliminate bowel movements
options.B: Synthetic fiber powders to speed up stomach emptying
options.C: Animal-derived fiber to build stronger intestinal walls
options.D: High-fiber foods to prevent chronic constipation

explanation: Well done! Because bowel movements tend to slow down with age, fiber is a simple superhero for adding bulk and preventing painful constipation. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T014#GNS227_U2_T014_h2)

question: Which vitamin and mineral combination is most crucial for keeping older adults' bones strong?

options.A: Iron and vitamin C
options.B: Sodium and vitamin A
options.C: Potassium and magnesium
options.D: Calcium and vitamin D

explanation: You got it! Calcium builds the bone, but vitamin D acts like the key that unlocks the door so the body can actually absorb that calcium. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T014#GNS227_U2_T014_h3)

question: Besides a poor diet, what is another very common cause of low iron levels in older adults?

options.A: Chronic gastrointestinal bleeding
options.B: Excessive absorption of iron in the stomach
options.C: Rapid destruction of iron by liver enzymes
options.D: High levels of stomach acid locking up iron

explanation: That's correct! Slow, hidden blood loss in the digestive tract (like from minor ulcers or polyps) is a frequent culprit behind low iron in elderly patients. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T014#GNS227_U2_T014_h3)

question: Why do older adults often become dehydrated without even realizing it?

options.A: The normal sensation of thirst becomes blunted with age
options.B: Their kidneys produce too much urine throughout the night
options.C: Cold beverages taste bitter to aging taste buds
options.D: Their bodies store twice as much water inside fat tissues

explanation: Spot on! As we age, our natural 'thirst trigger' gets a bit quiet, meaning older folks often won't feel thirsty even when their bodies are running low on water. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T014#GNS227_U2_T014_h4)

question: What is often one of the very first warning signs of dehydration in an elderly patient?

options.A: Sudden confusion or altered mental status
options.B: Swelling in the feet and lower ankles
options.C: Severe itching all over the skin surface
options.D: A sudden increase in appetite and weight

explanation: It's easy to miss, but sudden confusion is a classic red flag for dehydration in older adults! Always check hydration status when an elderly patient's mood or alertness changes. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T014#GNS227_U2_T014_h4)

question: What is the name of the popular screening tool used specifically to check nutritional risk in older adults?

options.A: Braden Skin Risk Scale
options.B: Glasgow Coma Scale
options.C: Mini Nutritional Assessment
options.D: Morse Fall Scale

explanation: That's the Mini Nutritional Assessment (MNA)! It's a quick, handy tool nurses use to catch nutrition risks early in older patients. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T014#GNS227_U2_T014_h5)

question: Which of these weight changes is considered a major red flag during a nutritional check-up?

options.A: Involuntary loss of 10 percent of body weight over six months
options.B: Gradual weight gain due to reduced physical activity
options.C: A stable weight fluctuating by one kilogram each week
options.D: A slight increase in body mass index after recovering from an illness

explanation: Spot on! Losing 10% or more of body weight in half a year is a serious warning sign of nutritional decline that requires immediate nursing attention. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T014#GNS227_U2_T014_h5)

question: How can a nurse best help a hospitalized older adult with severe arthritis eat on their own?

options.A: Insist that family members visit during every single mealtime
options.B: Feed the patient all meals to ensure they finish every single bite
options.C: Serve only pureed foods that require no physical chewing effort
options.D: Provide adaptive eating utensils like weighted handles or plate guards

explanation: Brilliant! Adaptive tools help work around stiff joints and tremors, letting patients keep their independence and dignity at mealtime. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T014#GNS227_U2_T014_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a helpful way to encourage eating in a frail older adult?

options.A: Forcing the patient to finish large meals within a strict time limit
options.B: Ensuring dentures are clean and placed in the mouth before mealtime
options.C: Creating a quiet, pleasant environment free from clinical distractions
options.D: Offering frequent small meals and nutrient-dense snacks throughout the day

explanation: You got it! Forcing big meals on someone with a poor appetite can be overwhelming. Smaller, frequent plates and a calm atmosphere work wonders instead! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T014#GNS227_U2_T014_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of human nutrition for body cells?

options.A: Increasing core body temperature overnight
options.B: Eliminating toxins through the renal system
options.C: Providing chemical substances for survival and repair
options.D: Regulating the speed of electrical nerve impulses

explanation: Nutrition supplies the raw chemical materials that cells need to stay alive, grow, and repair themselves daily. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T015#GNS227_U2_T015_h1)

question: Why is a continuous supply of nutrients necessary for human tissues?

options.A: Cells constantly carry out metabolic processes requiring fuel
options.B: The digestive tract stops working without fresh food hourly
options.C: Stored nutrients last for only a few minutes in the body
options.D: Tissues constantly expand in size throughout adult life

explanation: Cells never truly rest; they continually perform work that demands a steady influx of nutrients and energy. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T015#GNS227_U2_T015_h1)

question: Which macronutrient serves as the body's most rapid source of energy?

options.A: Carbohydrates
options.B: Fats
options.C: Vitamins
options.D: Proteins

explanation: Carbohydrates break down quickly into glucose, which cells rapidly use to create cellular energy. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T015#GNS227_U2_T015_h2)

question: A patient recovering from a large surgical wound requires tissue repair. Which macronutrient should the nurse ensure is adequately provided?

options.A: Carbohydrates
options.B: Fats
options.C: Proteins
options.D: Water

explanation: Proteins supply the amino acids required to build new tissue and heal surgical wounds effectively. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T015#GNS227_U2_T015_h2)

question: What is the primary function of vitamins in the human body?

options.A: Building thick outer walls around every body cell
options.B: Storing excess fat inside the abdominal cavity
options.C: Supplying the majority of daily caloric energy
options.D: Acting as coenzymes to regulate metabolic pathways

explanation: Vitamins do not provide calories, but they work as coenzymes to help chemical reactions run smoothly in the body. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T015#GNS227_U2_T015_h3)

question: Which of the following describes the difference between macronutrients and micronutrients?

options.A: Micronutrients are digested much faster than any macronutrient
options.B: Micronutrients are needed in smaller amounts and do not provide direct calories
options.C: Macronutrients are stored in bones while micronutrients float in blood
options.D: Macronutrients are only needed during childhood and growth phases

explanation: While macronutrients are consumed in large amounts for energy and structure, micronutrients are needed in tiny amounts to regulate body processes without supplying calories. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T015#GNS227_U2_T015_h3)

question: What is the primary role of water inside the human body?

options.A: Stimulating the production of red blood cells
options.B: Providing a dense reserve of long-term energy
options.C: Serving as the medium for all metabolic reactions
options.D: Preventing the breakdown of dietary proteins

explanation: Water provides the fluid environment where nutrients, wastes, and chemical reactions take place continuously. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T015#GNS227_U2_T015_h4)

question: A patient experiences severe dehydration. What immediate effect does this have on body function?

options.A: Sudden increase in muscle mass and bone density
options.B: Immediate conversion of fats into stored carbohydrates
options.C: Disruption of metabolic processes and electrolyte balance
options.D: Rapid overproduction of digestive enzymes in the gut

explanation: Without enough water, blood volume drops, electrolytes concentrate abnormally, and cellular chemical reactions slow down or fail. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T015#GNS227_U2_T015_h4)

question: What does Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) measure?

options.A: Calories used solely to digest a heavy meal
options.B: Total calories burned during intense physical exercise
options.C: Energy burned by the body at complete rest for vital functions
options.D: The speed at which the stomach empties into the intestines

explanation: BMR measures the baseline energy required to keep you alive while resting quietly. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T015#GNS227_U2_T015_h5)

question: How does overall energy balance affect a patient's body weight over time?

options.A: Consuming more calories than expended results in weight gain
options.B: BMR increases infinitely whenever extra food is eaten
options.C: Weight changes only occur if fluid balance is disturbed
options.D: Exercise alone determines weight without regard to food intake

explanation: Energy balance dictates that excess consumed calories are stored by the body, leading to weight gain. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T015#GNS227_U2_T015_h5)

question: Which group requires a higher proportion of protein and energy relative to body weight?

options.A: Sedentary older adults
options.B: Patients with chronic joint pain
options.C: Healthy middle-aged men
options.D: Infants and growing children

explanation: Rapid growth and cellular multiplication during childhood demand a high intake of building blocks like protein. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T015#GNS227_U2_T015_h6)

question: A patient with severe physical trauma from a motor vehicle accident is admitted to the ward. How does this physiological state affect their nutritional needs?

options.A: Metabolic demand increases, requiring more nutrients to prevent breakdown
options.B: Vitamins and minerals are no longer needed during acute healing
options.C: Water intake should be restricted to prevent cellular swelling
options.D: Caloric needs drop significantly because the patient is lying in bed

explanation: Trauma triggers a stress response that speeds up metabolism, requiring extra nutritional support to prevent muscle wasting. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T015#GNS227_U2_T015_h6)

question: Why must nurses consider a patient's cultural and socioeconomic background when planning a diet?

options.A: Culture dictates the exact BMR of every individual person
options.B: Religious practices completely eliminate the need for vitamins
options.C: Socioeconomic status determines how fast the stomach digests fats
options.D: These factors heavily influence food availability and traditional choices

explanation: Dietary habits are deeply tied to culture, beliefs, and economic access, which nurses must respect to ensure compliance. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T015#GNS227_U2_T015_h7)

question: What is a common socioeconomic barrier to good nutrition?

options.A: Inability to afford fresh, nutrient-dense food items
options.B: Excessive availability of free drinking water
options.C: A lack of personal interest in human anatomy
options.D: Too many cooking utensils in the household kitchen

explanation: Poverty and low income restrict access to quality food, often forcing reliance on cheap, calorie-dense foods with low nutritional value. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T015#GNS227_U2_T015_h7)

question: Which of the following measurements is considered an anthropometric assessment tool?

options.A: Body Mass Index (BMI)
options.B: Serum albumin blood test
options.C: Daily urine output volume
options.D: Blood pressure reading

explanation: Anthropometry involves physical measurements of the human body, such as height, weight, and BMI. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T015#GNS227_U2_T015_h8)

question: What is the main goal of performing a comprehensive nutritional assessment in a hospital setting?

options.A: Determining when the patient can be safely discharged home
options.B: Calculating the exact hospital bill for food services
options.C: Identifying existing or potential risks for malnutrition
options.D: Testing the patient's personal knowledge of grocery shopping

explanation: Assessment helps nurses catch nutritional deficits early so appropriate dietary interventions can be started promptly. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T015#GNS227_U2_T015_h8)

question: In community health nursing, what do we mean by a "food taboo"?

options.A: A cultural rule against eating certain foods
options.B: A government law controlling food prices
options.C: A medical prescription for weight loss
options.D: An allergic reaction to specific meals

explanation: A food taboo is simply a cultural or religious rule that says 'no' to eating certain edible items. You'll see this often in community postings! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T016#GNS227_U2_T016_h1)

question: Why is it important for a nurse to respect local food taboos rather than arguing with patients about them?

options.A: To build trust and encourage open communication with patients
options.B: To ensure the hospital saves money on meals
options.C: To follow strict government nursing regulations
options.D: To prove that traditional beliefs are always scientifically correct

explanation: When we respect our patients' beliefs instead of judging them, they feel safe and are more likely to share their real health habits with us. Great nursing is all about connection! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T016#GNS227_U2_T016_h1)

question: What is a major social reason why communities practice food taboos?

options.A: Preventing all forms of infectious diseases
options.B: Maintaining social order and group solidarity
options.C: Encouraging international food trade
options.D: Lowering the cost of agricultural production

explanation: Think of food rules as a way communities bond. Sharing the same dietary dos and don'ts brings people together and keeps their shared traditions strong. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T016#GNS227_U2_T016_h2)

question: How do feelings of disgust often shape food taboos in a society?

options.A: By making people lose their sense of taste completely
options.B: By increasing the body's need for protein
options.C: By associating scavenging animals with impurity and danger
options.D: By forcing individuals to eat more vegetables

explanation: When people view certain animals (like scavengers) as dirty or unsafe, that feeling of disgust turns into a long-lasting rule against eating them. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T016#GNS227_U2_T016_h2)

question: In some traditional settings, why are eggs and chicken meat sometimes withheld from young children?

options.A: Lack of available cooking oil in rural markets
options.B: Strict government laws against eating farm birds
options.C: Fear of causing speech delays, greed, or stubbornness
options.D: Belief that poultry meat causes high blood pressure

explanation: It's a common local myth! Elders sometimes worry that letting kids eat chicken or eggs will make them greedy or delay their talking. As nurses, we gently educate against this. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T016#GNS227_U2_T016_h3)

question: A mother denies her toddler eggs due to a local belief. What is the biggest danger of this practice?

options.A: Immediate development of a severe infectious disease
options.B: Complete immunity to childhood vitamin deficiencies
options.C: Deprivation of high-quality animal protein essential for growth
options.D: Rapid improvement in the child's daily speech patterns

explanation: Eggs are tiny powerhouses of protein and nutrients! Keeping them away from growing toddlers robs their bodies of what they need to build strong muscles and brains. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T016#GNS227_U2_T016_h3)

question: Which group in the community is usually hit hardest by nutritional food taboos?

options.A: Young adult working males
options.B: Pregnant and lactating women
options.C: Unmarried teenage boys
options.D: Elderly male community leaders

explanation: Expectant and breastfeeding mothers need extra nutrition, which unfortunately makes them prime targets for restrictive cultural rules. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T016#GNS227_U2_T016_h4)

question: Why do certain cultural practices place strict food bans on women during pregnancy?

options.A: To prevent birth deformities or ease future labor pains
options.B: To reduce the financial cost of feeding the family
options.C: To comply with international medical guidelines
options.D: To ensure the mother loses weight before delivery

explanation: These bans usually come from a place of protection—people genuinely worry that certain foods might harm the baby or make delivery difficult, even though science says otherwise. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T016#GNS227_U2_T016_h4)

question: What severe childhood malnutrition condition can happen when protein foods are restricted for too long?

options.A: Hypertension and stroke
options.B: Acute appendicitis
options.C: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
options.D: Kwashiorkor or marasmus

explanation: When a child's diet lacks proper protein and calories over time due to strict taboos, it sadly paves the way for protein-energy malnutrition like kwashiorkor. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T016#GNS227_U2_T016_h5)

question: Why might giving iron tablets fail to cure a patient's anemia if underlying food taboos are ignored?

options.A: The underlying cultural dietary restrictions continue to block vital nutrient intake
options.B: Iron tablets are completely useless against traditional beliefs
options.C: Patients always hide their medication from family members
options.D: Supplements make the patient develop an instant allergy to vegetables

explanation: Pills alone won't fix a problem driven by daily diet. If the patient is still culturally banned from eating iron-rich foods, the deficiency will just keep coming back. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T016#GNS227_U2_T016_h5)

question: What is the best way for a nurse to find out about hidden food taboos during a patient assessment?

options.A: Tell the patient that all traditional beliefs are wrong
options.B: Inspect the patient's kitchen without asking permission
options.C: Wait for laboratory tests to reveal all dietary habits
options.D: Ask open-ended questions about family dietary avoidances

explanation: Asking warm, open questions like 'Are there certain foods your family avoids eating?' helps patients open up without feeling judged or defensive. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T016#GNS227_U2_T016_h6)

question: You walk into the clinic and notice a toddler with swollen feet (edema) and sparse, discolored hair. What is your best next nursing action?

options.A: Assume the child has an infectious tropical disease and isolate them
options.B: Scold the mother for failing to feed the child expensive foreign foods
options.C: Discharge the child immediately with a prescription for multivitamins
options.D: Assess for protein-energy malnutrition and inquire about local food taboos

explanation: Those classic signs point right to malnutrition. A good nurse investigates gently, checking if restrictive family food habits are playing a role. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T016#GNS227_U2_T016_h6)

question: What is the primary aim of culturally sensitive nutrition counseling in nursing?

options.A: Forcing patients to abandon their cultural heritage completely
options.B: Convincing doctors to change hospital meal timetables
options.C: Replacing all local dishes with imported western food items
options.D: Finding acceptable local food substitutes that maintain good nutrition

explanation: We don't need to fight a patient's culture! Instead, we work with what they have, suggesting safe, affordable local foods that provide the exact same nutrients. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T016#GNS227_U2_T016_h7)

question: Who is most important to involve when trying to change harmful food taboos in a rural community?

options.A: Community elders and family heads
options.B: Children under the age of five years
options.C: Foreign tourists visiting the local market
options.D: International food manufacturing companies

explanation: In our communities, elders and family heads hold the keys to tradition. If you want sustainable change, you must bring them along on the health education journey! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T016#GNS227_U2_T016_h7)

question: What exactly do we mean by a "food myth" in healthcare?

options.A: A dietary belief that lacks scientific support
options.B: An official government nutrition guideline
options.C: A modern recipe created by clinical dietitians
options.D: A strict medical prescription for a disease

explanation: Food myths are unverified ideas about what food does to the body, passed along without scientific proof. Don't worry, once you spot them in clinical practice, they become much easier to address! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T017#GNS227_U2_T017_h1)

question: Why do nurses need to care about the food myths our patients believe?

options.A: Myths directly shape daily eating habits and health choices
options.B: Nurses are required to rewrite local recipe books
options.C: Patients will refuse all medications if they have food myths
options.D: Myths are always illegal to follow in a hospital setting

explanation: What people believe dictates what they put on their plates. Understanding this helps us guide patients better without making them feel judged! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T017#GNS227_U2_T017_h1)

question: Where do most traditional food beliefs and taboos originally come from?

options.A: From ancient survival experiences and local observations
options.B: From strict international food safety laws
options.C: From textbooks written by professional dietitians
options.D: From modern laboratory experiments conducted by scientists

explanation: Many food rules started long ago as clever ways to protect people from perceived dangers or explain natural events. History and culture run deep in our communities! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T017#GNS227_U2_T017_h2)

question: What part do community elders usually play in keeping traditional food beliefs alive?

options.A: They strictly enforce hospital dietary guidelines for patients
options.B: They pass down dietary rules and cultural heritage to younger generations
options.C: They import foreign ingredients to change local diets
options.D: They test new foods in scientific laboratories before cooking

explanation: Elders act as the keepers of tradition, sharing the stories and dietary practices that bind the community together. As nurses, we respect this heritage while promoting health! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T017#GNS227_U2_T017_h2)

question: Which common food is sometimes restricted for young children due to the old myth that it makes them steal?

options.A: Eggs
options.B: Yam
options.C: Beans
options.D: Rice

explanation: An old local myth falsely claims that feeding eggs to young children makes them prone to stealing. In reality, eggs are fantastic protein sources for growing kids! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T017#GNS227_U2_T017_h3)

question: A pregnant patient refuses to eat meat because she heard it causes birth defects. How should you handle this as her nurse?

options.A: Force her to eat the meat immediately during the clinic visit
options.B: Scold the patient for believing foolish stories
options.C: Recognize this as a cultural myth and gently offer safe protein alternatives
options.D: Ignore her diet since beliefs have no impact on pregnancy

explanation: Always respect your patient's background! Providing gentle, accurate education and helping them find alternative protein sources builds great trust. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T017#GNS227_U2_T017_h3)

question: Why are pregnant women and young children most vulnerable to harmful food myths?

options.A: They consume more processed foods than adults do
options.B: They have high nutritional demands for growth and development
options.C: They lack access to clean drinking water in all areas
options.D: They are legally required to follow traditional diets

explanation: Because their bodies need rich nutrients for rapid growth and pregnancy, restricting their diet can unfortunately lead to health setbacks. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T017#GNS227_U2_T017_h4)

question: What is a major health risk when growing infants are denied protein-rich foods because of cultural myths?

options.A: Faster physical growth
options.B: Improved natural immunity
options.C: Stronger bone density
options.D: Malnutrition and stunting

explanation: Withholding essential building blocks like protein from growing children frequently leads to malnutrition and delayed physical growth. Good nutrition education changes lives here! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T017#GNS227_U2_T017_h4)

question: How does evidence-based nutrition mainly differ from traditional food folklore?

options.A: It changes every single day without any consistency
options.B: It relies on scientific testing, trials, and biochemical data
options.C: It completely ignores what local communities like to eat
options.D: It focuses only on expensive imported foods from abroad

explanation: Evidence-based nutrition uses systematic scientific research to prove what foods actually do inside the human body, keeping our care safe and reliable. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T017#GNS227_U2_T017_h5)

question: Which of these traditional food practices actually goes hand-in-hand with modern science?

options.A: Combining grains and legumes for complete protein
options.B: Avoiding all liquids during a bout of severe diarrhea
options.C: Giving only sugary water to a newborn infant
options.D: Starving a patient completely to cure a high fever

explanation: Mixing grains and legumes (like rice and beans) is a brilliant traditional practice that supplies all essential amino acids our bodies need! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T017#GNS227_U2_T017_h5)

question: What is the best first step when a nurse finds out a patient believes a harmful food myth?

options.A: Listen openly to understand their reasoning without immediate judgment
options.B: Laugh at the idea to show how ridiculous the myth is
options.C: Hand them a lengthy research textbook to read
options.D: Refuse to treat the patient until they change their diet

explanation: Empathy and active listening build instant trust. When patients feel heard, they are much more open to your nursing guidance! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T017#GNS227_U2_T017_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a good way to help a patient move past a food myth?

options.A: Involving respected local community health volunteers
options.B: Acknowledging the good intentions behind the practice
options.C: Using simple analogies instead of heavy medical jargon
options.D: Directly insulting the patient's cultural background

explanation: Never insult a patient's heritage! It creates hostility and destroys the therapeutic nurse-patient relationship. Always keep your approach warm and respectful. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T017#GNS227_U2_T017_h6)

question: What is the main goal when giving culturally sensitive nutrition counseling?

options.A: To eliminate all traditional cooking methods from the community
options.B: To adapt healthy eating advice to fit the patient's local lifestyle and foods
options.C: To replace all local food items with expensive imported supplements
options.D: To force every patient to adopt a westernized diet style

explanation: Good nursing care works with what the patient already eats and enjoys, making healthy lifestyle changes realistic and sustainable. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T017#GNS227_U2_T017_h7)

question: A patient with high blood pressure loves strongly salted local seasonings. What is the most practical nursing approach?

options.A: Prescribe an expensive imported meal plan from another continent
options.B: Suggest reducing the salt gradually and using local aromatic herbs for flavor
options.C: Ignore their diet since salt intake has no effect on blood pressure
options.D: Tell the patient they must never taste local soup again for the rest of their life

explanation: Offering realistic tweaks like local herbs for flavor respects their food preferences while protecting their heart health. You've got this! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T017#GNS227_U2_T017_h7)

question: What is the main sign of a food fad?

options.A: It is a lifelong medical diet prescribed by a qualified physician.
options.B: It is a government-regulated nutrition program for school children.
options.C: It is a traditional cultural meal plan passed down for generations.
options.D: It is an intense and short-lived dietary trend without scientific backing.
