question: How should a bricklayer doing heavy manual labor in the hot Nigerian sun adjust their diet compared to a desk worker?

options.A: Decrease all food intake to prevent excessive sweating
options.B: Eliminate all carbohydrates to protect joint health
options.C: Rely exclusively on vitamin supplements instead of meals
options.D: Increase total energy and macronutrient intake to match high physical exertion

explanation: Heavy physical work burns through calories fast! They need more energy and macronutrients to keep up with the hard work. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T005#GNS227_U4_T005_h4)

question: What is the main drawback of using a 24-hour dietary recall?

options.A: It requires expensive laboratory equipment
options.B: It relies heavily on the patient's memory
options.C: It measures blood chemistry instead of food
options.D: It takes months to complete and analyze

explanation: People easily forget what they ate yesterday, which can lead to a few blank spots in a 24-hour recall! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T005#GNS227_U4_T005_h5)

question: How does keeping a food diary differ from doing a 24-hour dietary recall?

options.A: Food diaries measure blood levels instead of food intake
options.B: Food diaries rely entirely on long-term memory
options.C: Food diaries are only performed by specialized surgeons
options.D: Food diaries record items in real-time as they are consumed

explanation: Writing things down as you eat beats trying to remember everything at the end of the day! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T005#GNS227_U4_T005_h5)

question: Which of these is a direct health consequence of long-term undernutrition?

options.A: Abnormally elevated blood pressure readings
options.B: Rapid development of metabolic syndrome and obesity
options.C: Severe toxicity from excess fat-soluble vitamins
options.D: Weakened immune response and increased infection risk

explanation: Without enough nutrients, the body's defense cells can't fight off germs properly, leaving room for infections. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T005#GNS227_U4_T005_h6)

question: Why can taking too many fat-soluble vitamins become dangerous?

options.A: All vitamins contain high levels of dangerous dietary sodium
options.B: Excess vitamins immediately turn into stored body fat
options.C: High vitamin levels completely stop normal digestion
options.D: Fat-soluble vitamins can accumulate in the body and cause toxicity

explanation: Unlike water-soluble vitamins that wash right out, fat-soluble ones get stored in body tissues and can build up to harmful levels. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T005#GNS227_U4_T005_h6)

question: What is a major goal of food fortification programs in Nigeria (like adding vitamins to oil and flour)?

options.A: To reduce the financial cost of hospital buildings
options.B: To replace all local staple crops with imported grains
options.C: To increase the commercial shelf life of fresh meat
options.D: To combat widespread micronutrient deficiencies

explanation: Fortifying everyday foods helps protect whole communities from missing out on key vitamins and minerals. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T005#GNS227_U4_T005_h7)

question: A community health nurse is teaching a mother how to improve her family's protein intake using affordable local foods. What is the best advice?

options.A: Combine local plant sources like beans and maize to get complete proteins
options.B: Feed the family exclusively imported vitamin pills instead of meals
options.C: Avoid all local staple carbohydrates like yam and cassava completely
options.D: Rely only on expensive red meat imported from overseas

explanation: Pairing local plant foods like beans and maize gives you a complete protein combo without breaking the bank. Brilliant nursing care! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T005#GNS227_U4_T005_h7)

question: What unit of measurement is commonly used to express dietary energy?

options.A: Centimeters
options.B: Kilocalories
options.C: Milliliters
options.D: Milligrams

explanation: Dietary energy is measured in kilocalories, which are commonly called calories on food labels and in clinical practice. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h1)

question: When does a patient maintain a stable body weight?

options.A: Energy intake equals energy expenditure
options.B: Energy intake drops to zero for a day
options.C: Energy intake exceeds energy expenditure
options.D: Energy expenditure is higher than energy intake

explanation: Weight remains stable when the total calories consumed match the total calories burned by the body. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h1)

question: Which macronutrient provides the highest number of calories per gram?

options.A: Fat
options.B: Protein
options.C: Water
options.D: Carbohydrate

explanation: Fats are the most energy-dense nutrient, supplying nine kilocalories for every single gram consumed. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h2)

question: Why are dietary fats considered energy-dense?

options.A: They contain no carbon or hydrogen atoms
options.B: They convert directly into muscle without breakdown
options.C: They are digested much faster than carbs
options.D: They supply more than double the calories per gram compared to carbs or protein

explanation: You've got this! Fats give you nine calories per gram, while proteins and carbs only give four. That means fats pack much more energy into a smaller amount. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h2)

question: What is the largest component of total daily energy expenditure for most people?

options.A: Planned athletic exercise
options.B: Basal or resting metabolic rate
options.C: Adaptive thermogenesis
options.D: Thermic effect of food

explanation: Keeping your internal organs alive and functioning at rest takes up the vast majority of the calories you burn daily. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h3)

question: What does the 'thermic effect of food' mean?

options.A: Energy used to process and digest food
options.B: Heat produced when standing in cold weather
options.C: Calories burned during a heavy gym workout
options.D: Energy stored in fat tissue during starvation

explanation: Think of it this way: eating and digesting food actually makes your body work! The energy spent handling that food process is the thermic effect of food. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h3)

question: What body tissue is the primary driver of a person's metabolic rate?

options.A: Bone mineral matrix
options.B: Subcutaneous water
options.C: Adipose fat tissue
options.D: Lean muscle mass

explanation: Muscle tissue burns significantly more calories at rest than fat tissue, making muscle mass the main driver of metabolism. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h4)

question: Why do adult males typically have a higher resting metabolic rate than females of the same size?

options.A: Their digestive tract is physically longer
options.B: Their baseline body temperature is higher
options.C: Their brains require more glucose hourly
options.D: They generally have a higher percentage of lean muscle mass

explanation: Great job thinking through this! Men naturally tend to have more muscle mass than women, and since muscle burns more calories at rest, their baseline calorie need is higher. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h4)

question: Which macronutrient requires the most energy for the body to digest and process?

options.A: Refined oil
options.B: Protein
options.C: Simple sugar
options.D: Dietary fat

explanation: Protein has a high thermic effect, forcing the body to expend more calories during its breakdown and metabolism. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h5)

question: What does non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT) mean in daily life?

options.A: Energy used only during scheduled gym workouts
options.B: Calories burned through everyday movements like walking and fidgeting
options.C: Resting calories used by the heart while sleeping
options.D: Heat generated by a fever during an infection

explanation: NEAT is a fancy term for a simple idea: it's all the calories you burn just moving around during your normal day, outside of going to the gym! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h5)

question: What happens to the body during a state of positive energy balance?

options.A: It maintains a completely stable body weight
options.B: It burns stored fat to make up for a calorie deficit
options.C: It stores extra calories and gains weight
options.D: It stops all metabolic processes to save energy

explanation: When you take in more calories than you burn, the extra energy gets stored, primarily as fat, leading to weight gain. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h6)

question: A patient is recovering from major surgery and needs tissue repair. Which energy state is best?

options.A: Positive energy balance
options.B: Zero net energy balance
options.C: Complete metabolic shutdown
options.D: Severe negative energy balance

explanation: Healing takes work! Building new cells and repairing tissues require extra building blocks and calories, so a positive energy balance is just what the patient needs. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h6)

question: What does indirect calorimetry measure to calculate energy use?

options.A: Urinary nitrogen and fluid loss
options.B: Total body heat in a sealed room
options.C: Oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production
options.D: Electrical resistance of skin tissue

explanation: Spot on! Indirect calorimetry figures out how many calories someone is burning by analyzing the gases they breathe in and out. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h7)

question: Why are predictive equations used in hospital wards instead of direct calorimetry?

options.A: Calorimetry machines do not measure oxygen
options.B: Formulas are practical and easy to calculate using basic measurements
options.C: Calorimetry chambers are required by law
options.D: Equations are always 100% error-free for everyone

explanation: Using formulas gives nurses a fast, helpful estimate without needing complex or expensive test equipment right at the bedside. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h7)

question: What is a major risk of overfeeding a critically ill patient on a ventilator?

options.A: Extra carbon dioxide production making it harder to breathe off the ventilator
options.B: Total elimination of the need for IV fluids
options.C: Rapid healing of surgical wounds
options.D: A sudden drop in blood sugar levels

explanation: Giving too many calories—especially from carbs—makes the body produce extra carbon dioxide. This makes breathing much harder for a patient trying to come off a ventilator! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h8)

question: As a nurse, what is your most critical intervention to catch energy imbalances early in hospitalized patients?

options.A: Restricting family visits during meals
options.B: Performing regular and accurate weight measurements
options.C: Asking the patient their favorite food
options.D: Administering a daily multivitamin

explanation: You've got this! Tracking weight trends over time is the most reliable way for a nurse to see if a patient's calorie intake is matching what their body needs. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h8)

question: What do we mean when we talk about a person's caloric intake?

options.A: The total fluid volume consumed in a day
options.B: The amount of vitamins stored in body tissue
options.C: The total amount of energy consumed through food and drinks
options.D: The rate at which the body burns fat during sleep

explanation: Think of caloric intake simply as the fuel you take into your body through meals and drinks. You've got this! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h1)

question: What happens to a patient's body weight when their daily calorie intake matches what they burn?

options.A: Body weight increases rapidly
options.B: Body weight remains stable
options.C: Body weight decreases steadily
options.D: Metabolic rate stops functioning

explanation: When energy in equals energy out, your weight stays steady. Perfect balance! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h1)

question: In human nutrition, what exactly is a kilocalorie (kcal)?

options.A: The speed at which glucose enters the bloodstream
options.B: The heat needed to raise one kilogram of water by one degree Celsius
options.C: The amount of sodium dissolved in a liquid
options.D: The total protein weight inside a food item

explanation: A kilocalorie is just a unit of heat energy. It tells us the amount of energy needed to raise the temperature of a kilo of water by 1°C. Simple physics applied to food! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h2)

question: How do kilocalories (kcal) relate to kilojoules (kJ) on food packages?

options.A: Kilocalories and kilojoules are completely unrelated units
options.B: Kilojoules measure only liquid volume instead of energy
options.C: One kilojoule equals exactly 100 kilocalories
options.D: One kilocalorie equals about 4.184 kilojoules

explanation: Different countries use different units for energy. Just remember that 1 kcal is roughly equal to 4.184 kJ. You'll see both on nutrition labels! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h2)

question: Which macronutrient packs the most calories into every single gram?

options.A: Fat
options.B: Protein
options.C: Water
options.D: Carbohydrate

explanation: Fat gives us 9 calories per gram, while carbs and protein only give 4. That makes fat our most energy-dense nutrient! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h3)

question: A patient eats a snack with 10g of carbs, 5g of protein, and 4g of fat. What is their total calorie intake?

options.A: 60 kcal
options.B: 96 kcal
options.C: 76 kcal
options.D: 19 kcal

explanation: Let's break it down: Carbs (10 x 4 = 40), Protein (5 x 4 = 20), Fat (4 x 9 = 36). Add them up (40 + 20 + 36) to get 96 total calories. You're doing great with math! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h3)

question: What is Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR)?

options.A: Energy required for vital organ function at complete rest
options.B: Calories burned only during heavy weightlifting
options.C: Total daily calories burned including all movement
options.D: The energy used solely to digest food particles

explanation: BMR is the baseline energy your body needs just to keep your heart pumping and lungs breathing while you rest quietly. No movement required! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h4)

question: What does the thermic effect of food (TEF) refer to?

options.A: The heat lost through the skin during a fever
options.B: The calories burned during cardiovascular exercise
options.C: The basal energy used by the liver during sleep
options.D: The energy used to process and digest nutrients

explanation: Your body actually burns calories just chewing, digesting, and processing food. That's what we call TEF! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h4)

question: What is the most accurate way to measure energy use in a critical care patient?

options.A: Indirect calorimetry
options.B: Skinfold caliper tests
options.C: Standard food diaries
options.D: Body mass index charts

explanation: Indirect calorimetry measures the gases a patient breathes out to figure out their exact calorie needs. It's the gold standard in the ICU! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h5)

question: Why do nurses and dietitians use activity multipliers along with a patient's BMR?

options.A: To correct for errors in food label calorie counts
options.B: To determine the patient's exact vitamin requirements
options.C: To account for daily movement and exercise energy costs
options.D: To calculate the exact amount of daily water loss

explanation: BMR only covers resting in bed. Activity multipliers help us estimate the extra calories burned walking around or doing physical therapy. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h5)

question: What does it mean when a patient is in a positive energy balance?

options.A: Caloric expenditure is greater than caloric intake
options.B: Total body weight remains completely unchanging
options.C: Caloric intake and expenditure are perfectly equal
options.D: Caloric intake is greater than caloric expenditure

explanation: When you take in more food energy than your body burns, the extra energy is stored. That's a positive energy balance! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h6)

question: What is a major risk for a hospitalized patient who stays in a severe negative energy balance for too long?

options.A: Excessive fluid retention in lower extremities
options.B: Elevated resting metabolic rate above normal limits
options.C: Rapid increase in subcutaneous fat stores
options.D: Lean muscle wasting and delayed wound healing

explanation: When patients don't get enough calories, their bodies start breaking down muscle for fuel, making it hard for wounds to heal. Nutrition is vital care! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h6)

question: Why should nurses check and document what is left on a patient's meal tray rather than just taking it away?

options.A: To speed up the collection of dirty kitchen dishes
options.B: To calculate the precise cost of hospital food items
options.C: To ensure accurate tracking of actual calories consumed
options.D: To prevent patients from sharing food with visitors

explanation: An empty tray doesn't always mean the patient ate the food! Direct observation helps us chart their true nutritional intake accurately. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h7)

question: What should a nurse do if a patient consistently eats less than 30 percent of their food?

options.A: Wait two weeks to see if appetite returns on its own
options.B: Notify the dietitian and consider nutritional support options
options.C: Tell the patient that eating is mandatory for discharge
options.D: Remove all meal trays immediately without documenting intake

explanation: Poor intake puts patients at risk for malnutrition. Always team up with the dietitian early to help your patient get the nutrition they need! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T007#GNS227_U4_T007_h7)

question: What unit of measurement is commonly used to express energy expenditure in human nutrition?

options.A: Centimeters
options.B: Kilocalories
options.C: Milligrams
options.D: Milliliters

explanation: Energy in human nutrition is measured in kilocalories, which people commonly call calories. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h1)

question: What happens when a person's daily energy expenditure is greater than their calorie intake?

options.A: The body uses stored energy, leading to weight loss
options.B: The body stores the extra energy as fat
options.C: The metabolic rate automatically drops to zero
options.D: The body stops using energy completely

explanation: You've got this! When you burn more calories than you eat, your body simply taps into its stored reserves for fuel, which leads to weight loss. Simple math of the body! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h1)

question: What does the basal metabolic rate measure?

options.A: Total calories burned during heavy physical exercise
options.B: Extra calories burned due to cold weather exposure
options.C: Energy used specifically to digest a large meal
options.D: Minimum calories needed for basic life functions at rest

explanation: BMR is the baseline energy required by the body to sustain vital organs while completely at rest. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h2)

question: Why do clinicians often use resting metabolic rate (RMR) instead of basal metabolic rate (BMR)?

options.A: It completely excludes the energy used by internal organs
options.B: It is always identical to total daily energy expenditure
options.C: It measures the exact calories burned during running
options.D: It requires fewer strict laboratory conditions to measure

explanation: Great job! RMR is much more practical in hospital and clinic settings because it doesn't force the patient to go through a strict 12-hour fast and absolute rest like BMR does. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h2)

question: What is the thermic effect of food?

options.A: Total calories burned while sleeping at night
options.B: Energy used to digest, absorb, and process consumed nutrients
options.C: Heat produced when a person exercises outdoors
options.D: Extra vitamins lost through normal digestion

explanation: TEF represents the energy cost of handling food within the digestive and metabolic tracts. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h3)

question: Which nutrient takes the most energy for your body to process and digest?

options.A: Protein
options.B: Fat
options.C: Simple sugars
options.D: Water

explanation: Spot on! Protein has a high thermic effect, meaning your body actually burns a good chunk of calories just breaking it down. Eat protein, burn energy! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h3)

question: What does the acronym NEAT stand for in energy expenditure?

options.A: Non-exercise activity thermogenesis
options.B: Nutritional energy and tissue
options.C: Net enteral absorption time
options.D: Normal electrolyte and acid test

explanation: NEAT stands for non-exercise activity thermogenesis, covering all daily movements outside of formal workouts. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h4)

question: Which of these everyday activities is a classic example of NEAT (Non-Exercise Activity Thermogenesis)?

options.A: Running a scheduled marathon on Saturday morning
options.B: Lifting heavy weights at the gym for an hour
options.C: Pacing up and down the hospital hallway while on duty
options.D: Swimming laps in a competitive swimming pool

explanation: Exactly! As student nurses on clinical duty, all that walking, pacing, and running around the ward counts as NEAT—unplanned movement outside the gym! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h4)

question: Which tissue type burns more calories at rest?

options.A: Bone matrix
options.B: Blood plasma
options.C: Muscle tissue
options.D: Adipose tissue

explanation: Muscle is metabolically active tissue that burns more energy at rest than fat (adipose) tissue. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h5)

question: Why do biological males typically have a higher resting metabolic rate than biological females of the same weight?

options.A: They usually have a higher proportion of muscle mass
options.B: Their digestive tracts absorb fewer calories overall
options.C: They consume more water throughout the day
options.D: They have lower body temperatures on average

explanation: You got it! Because muscle burns more energy than fat at rest, having a higher muscle mass naturally bumps up the baseline metabolic rate. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h5)

question: What does direct calorimetry measure to determine energy expenditure?

options.A: Heat produced by the body
options.B: Carbon dioxide exhaled in breath
options.C: Oxygen inhaled through a mask
options.D: Nitrogen lost in urine samples

explanation: Direct calorimetry calculates energy use by measuring the actual heat given off by a person inside a special chamber. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h6)

question: What is the main benefit of using predictive equations in clinical settings?

options.A: They eliminate the need to know the patient's weight
options.B: They provide the absolute most accurate measurement possible
options.C: They are quick and easy to calculate without special equipment
options.D: They directly measure the heat released from human skin

explanation: Spot on! When you don't have expensive laboratory gadgets in the ward, predictive equations let nurses quickly estimate a patient's calorie needs using basic measurements. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h6)

question: What happens to a patient's metabolic rate during severe physiological stress like major trauma or sepsis?

options.A: It remains completely unchanged
options.B: It fluctuates only during sleep
options.C: It drops to zero instantly
options.D: It increases significantly

explanation: Severe physical trauma and infections trigger a hypermetabolic state that dramatically increases energy expenditure. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h7)

question: A patient with severe burn wounds is at risk of poor healing if which nutritional goal is missed?

options.A: Meeting their increased energy expenditure needs
options.B: Eliminating all dietary fats from their meals
options.C: Reducing their daily protein consumption
options.D: Restricting their fluid intake to prevent swelling

explanation: Brilliant! Burn patients undergo massive stress and need plenty of calories and protein. If we don't meet their soaring energy needs, their tissues simply won't heal properly. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T008#GNS227_U4_T008_h7)

question: Why are deep yellow and orange vegetables so good for your health?

options.A: It speeds up the absorption of glucose in the gut
options.B: It binds directly to cholesterol in the stomach
options.C: It acts as a precursor to vitamin A in the body
options.D: It serves as the main structural protein for cell walls

explanation: Great job! Beta-carotene is simply a plant pigment that your body turns into vitamin A, which keeps your eyes and immune system strong. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h1)

question: How does fiber from vegetables help keep your blood sugar steady?

options.A: By slowing down the rate at which glucose is absorbed in the gut
options.B: By directly destroying excess sugar molecules in the bloodstream
options.C: By converting surplus glucose into stored body fat for later use
options.D: By stimulating the pancreas to produce more insulin immediately

explanation: You've got this! Fiber slows down digestion, which stops sugar from rushing into your blood all at once and causing sudden spikes. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h1)

question: Which group of vegetables is famous for helping your liver clear out toxins?

options.A: Cruciferous vegetables
options.B: Root and tuber vegetables
options.C: Fruiting vegetables
options.D: Leafy green vegetables

explanation: Spot on! Vegetables like cabbage and broccoli belong to the cruciferous family and contain special compounds that give your liver a helping hand. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h2)

question: A patient asks which vegetable group is packed with vitamin C and lycopene. What's your best reply?

options.A: Leafy greens like spinach and pumpkin leaves
options.B: Bulb vegetables like onions and garlic
options.C: Fruiting vegetables like tomatoes and peppers
options.D: Root vegetables like carrots and beets

explanation: Exactly! Tomatoes, peppers, and garden eggs grow from the flowering parts of plants and are loaded with vitamin C and antioxidants. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h2)

question: What is the daily amount of vegetables recommended to help adults stay healthy?

options.A: About 400 grams or roughly five servings
options.B: At least 1 kilogram divided into ten meals
options.C: Only 50 grams taken once a week
options.D: Exactly 100 grams or one large serving

explanation: Well done! Health guidelines generally suggest aiming for around 400 grams of fruits and veggies daily to keep chronic illnesses at bay. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h3)

question: Why do pregnant women need to eat plenty of dark green leafy vegetables?

options.A: They supply essential folate and iron needed for fetal neural development and blood volume
options.B: They completely eliminate morning sickness by neutralizing stomach acid
options.C: They replace the need for all routine prenatal vitamin supplements
options.D: They prevent the mother from gaining any excess weight during the pregnancy

explanation: You're doing great! Dark greens give moms-to-be iron for extra blood and folate to protect the baby's developing brain and spine. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h3)

question: Which popular Nigerian vegetable is well-known as a fantastic plant source of iron?

options.A: Fluted pumpkin leaves (Ugu)
options.B: Jute mallow (Ewedu)
options.C: Waterleaf
options.D: African garden egg

explanation: Correct! Ugu is a local favorite that packs a serious iron punch, making it brilliant for fighting off anemia. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h4)

question: Why do cooks love adding waterleaf to traditional Nigerian soups and stews?

options.A: It turns the broth into a solid gel when allowed to cool down
options.B: It serves as a strong preservative to keep soups from spoiling quickly
options.C: It acts as a natural thickening agent while adding moisture and vitamins
options.D: It completely replaces the need for adding palm oil to the pot

explanation: Spot on! Waterleaf breaks down nicely during cooking to give soups a rich texture while boosting the vitamin content. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h4)

question: Which vitamins are most easily lost when vegetables are boiled in too much water?

options.A: Inert plant fibers like cellulose and lignin
options.B: Water-soluble vitamins like vitamin C and B vitamins
options.C: Fat-soluble vitamins like vitamin A and vitamin E
options.D: Structural minerals like calcium and iron

explanation: You got it! Vitamins C and B love water, so they dissolve right out of the veggies and into the cooking pot. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h5)

question: Why is it smart not to throw away the broth after boiling vegetables?

options.A: It slows down digestion so much that hunger never returns
options.B: It neutralizes all harmful bacteria that may have survived the cooking process
options.C: It recaptures water-soluble vitamins and minerals that leaked out during boiling
options.D: It provides all the dietary protein required for the day in one serving

explanation: Brilliant! Drinking the soup broth ensures you don't lose all those valuable vitamins that leaked out into the water. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h5)

question: What is a simple, practical way to store extra green vegetables when electricity is unreliable?

options.A: Sealing in airtight glass jars with heavy salt
options.B: Soaking them continuously in vinegar
options.C: Sun-drying or blanching
options.D: Deep-freezing for three years

explanation: Correct! Sun-drying and blanching are time-tested ways to keep your veggies from spoiling without needing a fridge. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h6)

question: Why is buying vegetables that are currently "in season" a smart strategy?

options.A: It ensures the vegetables have zero water content inside them
options.B: It guarantees that the vegetables will never contain any natural toxins
options.C: It makes fresh produce more affordable and readily available in the local market
options.D: It eliminates the need to wash the produce before cooking it

explanation: Well reasoned! When crops are in season, they are abundant and cheap, making healthy eating much easier on the wallet. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h6)

question: What is the best approach when a nurse gives dietary advice to a patient with a chronic condition?

options.A: Telling the patient to rely entirely on vitamin supplements instead of food
options.B: Focusing solely on what foods the patient must completely ban from the house
options.C: Tailoring advice to fit the patient's cultural background, finances, and lifestyle
options.D: Handing out a strict, pre-printed meal plan that cannot be changed

explanation: Spot on! Advice only works if it fits into the patient's real life, budget, and cultural preferences. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h7)

question: A patient with type 2 diabetes needs help managing their meals. What is a great, simple tip to share first?

options.A: Replace all water intake with fresh vegetable juices only
options.B: Cook your vegetables without any seasoning or oil whatsoever
options.C: Stop eating all forms of food for two days of the week
options.D: Fill half of your meal plate with non-starchy, colorful vegetables

explanation: You nailed it! The plate method is a fantastic, visual way to help patients control portions and get enough fiber without stressful calorie counting. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T009#GNS227_U4_T009_h7)

question: Which mineral found in fruits helps to lower and regulate blood pressure?

options.A: Magnesium
options.B: Calcium
options.C: Potassium
options.D: Sodium

explanation: Spot on! Potassium is fantastic for the heart because it helps ease tension in your blood vessel walls, keeping your blood pressure steady. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T010#GNS227_U4_T010_h1)

question: How does vitamin C from fruits help your body use iron better?

options.A: It breaks down complex proteins in animal meat
options.B: It directly converts red blood cells into hemoglobin
options.C: It prevents the liver from storing excess iron
options.D: It enhances the absorption of non-heme iron in the gut

explanation: You got it! Vitamin C teams up with plant-based iron in your tummy, making it much easier for your body to absorb. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T010#GNS227_U4_T010_h1)

question: What is the recommended daily target for fruit and vegetable portions for adults?

options.A: Exactly ten portions
options.B: Only one single portion
options.C: As many as possible without limit
options.D: At least five portions

explanation: Correct! Aiming for at least five portions a day is a wonderful, simple habit to keep your body healthy and strong. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T010#GNS227_U4_T010_h2)

question: A pregnant woman asks why she needs more fruit servings now. What is the best response?

options.A: Eating more fruit is only needed to prevent weight loss in the third trimester.
options.B: You must replace all your meals with fresh fruit juices during pregnancy.
options.C: Your body needs higher vitamins and fiber to support increased metabolic demands and growth.
options.D: Pregnancy completely stops your body from absorbing vitamins from regular food.

explanation: Well done! Pregnancy is a time of double duty—maternal tissues and the growing baby both need extra vitamins and fiber. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T010#GNS227_U4_T010_h2)

question: Why is a standard serving size for dried fruit much smaller than fresh fruit?

options.A: Dried fruit expands rapidly inside the human stomach
options.B: Manufacturers add synthetic preservatives to dried fruits
options.C: Water removal concentrates its natural sugars and calories
options.D: The digestive system cannot process dried fruit easily

explanation: That's right! Without water taking up space, dried fruit is packed tightly with natural sugars, so a smaller handful is plenty. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T010#GNS227_U4_T010_h3)

question: Which of these is a standard single serving of fresh fruit for an adult?

options.A: Five liters of blended fruit smoothie
options.B: One tiny slice of dried pineapple
options.C: Two large bowls of sliced watermelon
options.D: One medium-sized whole orange

explanation: Spot on! One medium-sized whole fruit—like an orange, banana, or apple—makes a perfect single portion. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T010#GNS227_U4_T010_h3)

question: Why do whole fruits cause a slower, safer rise in blood sugar than fruit juices?

options.A: Whole fruits contain zero natural sugars unlike juice
options.B: The intact fiber slows down digestion and sugar absorption
options.C: Teexh enzymes block sugar from entering the bloodstream
options.D: Stomach acid instantly destroys all fruit sugars

explanation: Correct! The natural fiber in whole fruits acts like a speed bump, helping your body absorb the sugar nice and slowly. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T010#GNS227_U4_T010_h4)

question: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of choosing whole fruit over fruit juice?

options.A: Encouraging healthy chewing and saliva flow
options.B: Providing a concentrated dose of liquid sugar
options.C: Promoting a feeling of fullness after eating
options.D: Supplying beneficial dietary fiber

explanation: You nailed it! Concentrated liquid sugar is actually found in juices, and it can cause your blood sugar to spike quickly. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T010#GNS227_U4_T010_h4)

question: What is a major advantage of eating seasonal local fruits here in Nigeria?

options.A: They contain no natural carbohydrates at all
options.B: They last indefinitely without refrigeration
options.C: They are imported directly from foreign countries
options.D: They are more affordable and readily available

explanation: Exactly! Buying local and in-season means fresher fruits that are kind to your wallet and easy to find in our markets. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T010#GNS227_U4_T010_h5)

question: Which of these is an indigenous fruit commonly found in Nigerian local markets?

options.A: African star apple (agbalumo)
options.B: Imported green kiwi fruit
options.C: Fresh arctic cloudberries
options.D: Temperated climate wild blueberries

explanation: Correct! Agbalumo is a beloved seasonal Nigerian fruit packed with wonderful vitamins and fiber. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T010#GNS227_U4_T010_h5)

question: A patient complains that fresh fruits spoil too quickly. What practical advice can you give?

options.A: Soak the fruits in salty water for forty-eight hours.
options.B: Stop buying fresh fruit completely and drink soda instead.
options.C: Leave all fruits uncovered under direct sunlight every day.
options.D: Freeze ripe fruits or store them properly to extend their usable shelf life.

explanation: Spot on! Proper refrigeration or freezing stops food from going waste, helping patients enjoy their fresh produce longer. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T010#GNS227_U4_T010_h6)

question: How does buying fruits in their natural season help families on a tight budget?

options.A: Farmers give away all seasonal fruits for free to hospitals
options.B: Seasonal fruits never require washing or preparation
options.C: Abundant supply during peak season drives market prices down
options.D: Government laws make out-of-season fruits illegal to sell

explanation: You got it! When farmers harvest a lot of a fruit during its peak season, the market price drops, making healthy eating budget-friendly. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T010#GNS227_U4_T010_h6)

question: What is the main building role of lipids in our bodies?

options.A: Building the outer layer of every cell
options.B: Acting as enzymes to speed up reactions
options.C: Providing quick energy for the brain
options.D: Carrying water-soluble vitamins in the blood

explanation: You've got this! Phospholipids and cholesterol act like tiny bricks that form the protective wall (membrane) around all our cells. Great job! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h1)

question: Why do we actually need dietary fats to absorb certain vitamins?

options.A: Fat binds directly to water-soluble vitamins
options.B: Fat makes the stomach produce more acid
options.C: Vitamins A, D, E, and K dissolve in fat
options.D: Fat stops the liver from destroying vitamins

explanation: Think of fat as the vehicle that carries vitamins A, D, E, and K through your gut so your body can use them. Without fat, these vitamins just pass right through! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h1)

question: What chemical feature makes a fatty acid 'saturated'?

options.A: It only comes from plant sources
options.B: It stays completely liquid at room temperature
options.C: It has no double bonds between carbon atoms
options.D: It has multiple double bonds in the chain

explanation: Saturated fats are packed tightly together with single bonds only, which is why butter (a saturated fat) stays solid at room temperature! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h2)

question: A patient with high cholesterol asks which fat to avoid completely. What should you tell them?

options.A: Trans fats
options.B: Omega-3 fatty acids
options.C: Polyunsaturated oils
options.D: Monounsaturated fats

explanation: Trans fats are artificial troublemakers! They raise bad cholesterol and lower the good kind, so it's best to avoid them for a healthy heart. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h2)

question: What is the recommended daily percentage range for total fat intake in healthy adults?
explanation: Aiming for 20% to 35% of daily calories from fats keeps adults energized and healthy without overdoing it. You're doing great! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h3)

question: Why do health guidelines look closely at the *type* of fat we eat, rather than just total grams?

options.A: The body cannot digest saturated fats at all
options.B: Unsaturated fats provide zero energy
options.C: Different fats have very different effects on heart health
options.D: Total fat intake has no effect on body weight

explanation: Not all fats are enemies! While trans fats clog arteries, healthy fats like olive oil protect your heart. It's all about quality over quantity. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h3)

question: What is a common long-term effect of eating too many trans and saturated fats?

options.A: Atherosclerosis and higher heart risk
options.B: Stronger storage of vitamins in bones
options.C: Less inflammation in the arteries
options.D: Better production of good cholesterol

explanation: Eating too many bad fats causes fatty plaque to build up in the arteries (atherosclerosis), making the heart work much harder. Good catch! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h4)

question: Which problem is most likely to happen if someone has a severe lack of dietary fat?

options.A: Dangerous spikes in blood sugar
options.B: Trouble absorbing vitamins A, D, E, and K
options.C: An enlarged thyroid gland
options.D: Too much good cholesterol in the blood

explanation: Remember, fat-soluble vitamins need dietary fat to get absorbed! Without enough fat, deficiency symptoms start to show up. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h4)

question: A patient with high cholesterol uses butter for all their cooking. What heart-healthy swap can you suggest?

options.A: Coconut oil
options.B: Olive or canola oil
options.C: Palm oil
options.D: Solid shortening

explanation: Liquid plant oils like olive or canola are rich in unsaturated fats, making them fantastic, heart-friendly swaps for solid butter! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h5)

question: Why is teaching patients to read food labels a great nursing skill for fat management?

options.A: It proves processed foods are dangerous
options.B: It helps them spot hidden trans and saturated fats
options.C: It guarantees quick weight loss
options.D: It means they never need to see a dietitian again

explanation: Food labels can be tricky! Teaching patients to read them empowers them to catch hidden bad fats lurking in packaged snacks. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h5)

question: What exactly are intrinsic sugars?

options.A: Sugars naturally bound inside the cell walls of whole foods
options.B: Chemical preservatives used to extend shelf life in drinks
options.C: Refined sweeteners added to foods during factory processing
options.D: Artificial sweeteners that contain zero calories

explanation: You can think of intrinsic sugars as the good guys! They are safely locked inside whole, unprocessed foods like fruits and vegetables, right alongside healthy fiber. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T012#GNS227_U4_T012_h1)

question: Why do intrinsic sugars digest much slower than free sugars?

options.A: They bind to red blood cells and delay energy release
options.B: They are protected by the natural cellular structure and fiber of the food
options.C: They bypass the stomach and enter the small intestine immediately
options.D: They require no digestive enzymes to break them down into glucose

explanation: Because the fiber and cell walls are intact, your digestive system has to put in extra work. This slows down how fast sugar enters your bloodstream, giving you steady energy! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T012#GNS227_U4_T012_h1)

question: Which organ gets overwhelmed and converts surplus dietary sugars into fat?

options.A: Stomach
options.B: Kidneys
options.C: Pancreas
options.D: Liver

explanation: Your liver handles the heavy lifting when processing dietary sugars. When it gets overloaded, it converts those extra sugars directly into fat molecules. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T012#GNS227_U4_T012_h2)

question: How does eating too much sugar over a long time lead to insulin resistance?

options.A: Sugar molecules coat the pancreas and permanently stop it from making any digestive enzymes
options.B: Constant high blood sugar forces the pancreas to oversecrete insulin until body cells stop responding
options.C: High sugar levels destroy every insulin receptor in the liver instantly
options.D: The kidneys block all insulin from entering the bloodstream to protect the heart

explanation: Imagine constantly shouting at someone—eventually, they stop listening! High glucose levels force your pancreas to pump out so much insulin that your body cells eventually tune it out. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T012#GNS227_U4_T012_h2)

question: What is the WHO's strong recommendation for daily free sugar intake?

options.A: Less than 10%
options.B: Less than 25%
options.C: Exactly 15%
options.D: More than 30%

explanation: The World Health Organization (WHO) advises keeping free sugars below 10% of your total daily energy intake to help prevent health issues like obesity and tooth decay. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T012#GNS227_U4_T012_h3)

question: For an adult needing 2,000 calories a day, roughly how many grams of free sugar is the stricter 5% WHO target?

options.A: 25 grams
options.B: 200 grams
options.C: 100 grams
options.D: 50 grams

explanation: Ten percent of 2,000 calories is 200 calories (or 50 grams of sugar). The conditional 5% target cuts that amount right in half to just 25 grams! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T012#GNS227_U4_T012_h3)

question: When reading ingredient labels, which suffix usually tells you an ingredient is a sugar?

options.A: -ase
options.B: -ose
options.C: -ite
options.D: -one

explanation: Spotting a sneaky sugar is easier when you know the language! Most simple sugars end in '-ose', like sucrose, lactose, and glucose. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T012#GNS227_U4_T012_h4)

question: Why do food manufacturers sometimes use multiple different names for sugar on a single ingredient list?

options.A: To divide the total amount so individual sugars appear further down the weight-based ingredient list
options.B: To make the product taste better by combining artificial and natural sweeteners together
options.C: To prevent the food from spoiling too quickly on supermarket shelves
options.D: To comply with strict international laws requiring chemical names for every single food item

explanation: It's a clever marketing trick! By splitting sugar into three or four different names, manufacturers can scatter them down the list so the product looks healthier than it really is. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T012#GNS227_U4_T012_h4)

question: What is the most effective first step a nurse can suggest to help a patient cut down on hidden sugars?

options.A: Eating only raw vegetables for breakfast and lunch
options.B: Replacing sugary sodas and packaged fruit juices with plain water
options.C: Eliminating all complex carbohydrates from every meal
options.D: Switching from white table sugar to organic raw honey

explanation: Sugary drinks are the biggest source of hidden calories in most diets. Swapping them for water is the easiest and most powerful change a patient can make! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T012#GNS227_U4_T012_h5)

question: A patient wants to bake a healthier cake with less refined sugar. What is a great nursing suggestion?

options.A: Use mashed ripe bananas or unsweetened applesauce to add natural sweetness and moisture
options.B: Add artificial chemical cleaners to make the dough rise faster
options.C: Double the amount of salt to block the bitter taste of unsweetened flour
options.D: Replace sugar with extra drops of liquid vegetable oil

explanation: Mashed fruits are fantastic baking substitutes! They bring natural sweetness and moisture thanks to their intrinsic sugars and fiber, keeping the cake delicious without refined sugar. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T012#GNS227_U4_T012_h5)

question: Why do nurses use the idea of a 'standard drink' instead of just counting glasses or bottles?

options.A: Serving sizes and alcohol strengths vary widely between different beverages
options.B: It makes tax calculations easier for local health authorities
options.C: Spirits contain no pure alcohol when mixed with water
options.D: Bottles of wine always contain exactly one standard serving

explanation: Not all drinks are poured equal! A big mug of stout packs way more punch than a small glass of wine. Using standard drinks helps patients track their real intake accurately. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T013#GNS227_U4_T013_h1)

question: A patient drinks two large mugs of strong craft beer every evening. Why might this be more alcohol than they realize?

options.A: Large mugs automatically convert alcohol into non-toxic carbohydrates
options.B: Beer loses its alcohol content completely when served in a mug
options.C: Fermented beverages do not register on standard liver enzyme tests
options.D: Craft beer usually contains a higher alcohol percentage and larger volume than a standard drink

explanation: A large mug holds way more liquid than a standard serving, and craft brews are often extra strong. One big mug can easily equal two or more standard drinks! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T013#GNS227_U4_T013_h1)

question: What is a main benefit of having several alcohol-free days each week?

options.A: To completely reverse any genetic predisposition to liver failure
options.B: To double the recommended intake limits on the remaining days
options.C: To ensure the body stores enough pure ethanol for energy
options.D: To prevent tolerance buildup and lower the risk of dependency

explanation: Giving the liver and the habit a break helps prevent your body from getting too used to daily alcohol. It's a great way to keep drinking habits in check! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T013#GNS227_U4_T013_h2)

question: What is the current stance of global health organizations regarding a completely safe level of alcohol consumption?

options.A: Safe levels depend entirely on a person's physical height and weight
options.B: No level of alcohol consumption is considered entirely free of health risks
options.C: Only heavy spirits carry health risks, while wine and beer are completely safe
options.D: Consuming up to five drinks daily provides proven cardiovascular protection

explanation: Even though people enjoy a drink socially, health experts note that any amount of alcohol carries some degree of risk to the body, especially over time. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T013#GNS227_U4_T013_h2)

question: Why does a woman usually reach a higher blood alcohol concentration than a man after drinking the exact same amount?

options.A: Men possess specialized liver filters that instantly destroy ethanol
options.B: Female digestive tracts absorb alcohol at a slower, safer rate
options.C: Women generally have less body water and lower gastric enzyme activity
options.D: Men store all excess alcohol in fat tissue instead of the bloodstream

explanation: Because women typically have less total body water and lower levels of stomach enzymes to break down alcohol, more of it enters the bloodstream faster. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T013#GNS227_U4_T013_h3)

question: A man and a woman of the same weight each have two standard drinks. What is the most likely result?

options.A: The male patient will absorb the alcohol much faster than the female patient
options.B: Neither patient will absorb any alcohol into their systemic circulation
options.C: The female patient will have a noticeably higher blood alcohol concentration
options.D: Both patients will have the exact same blood alcohol concentration

explanation: Body composition matters! Differences in body water and metabolism mean women generally hit higher blood alcohol levels than men from the exact same drink. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T013#GNS227_U4_T013_h3)

question: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, a serious memory problem linked to heavy drinking, is caused by a shortage of which nutrient?

options.A: Ascorbic acid (Vitamin C)
options.B: Thiamine (Vitamin B1)
options.C: Calcium and magnesium
options.D: Iron and folic acid

explanation: Heavy drinking messes with how the body absorbs nutrients. Lacking Vitamin B1 (thiamine) can lead to severe, lasting brain issues if not caught and treated early. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T013#GNS227_U4_T013_h4)

question: Which of these is a classic long-term heart problem tied to heavy, chronic drinking?

options.A: Permanent stabilization of heart valves
options.B: Cardiomyopathy and hypertension
options.C: Significantly lowered resting pulse rate
options.D: Increased production of red blood cells

explanation: Over time, heavy drinking weakens the heart muscle (cardiomyopathy) and drives up blood pressure (hypertension). Take care of that ticker! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T013#GNS227_U4_T013_h4)

question: Why must pregnant patients completely avoid alcohol at any stage of pregnancy?

options.A: Gestational hormones turn ethanol into a strong muscle relaxant for the baby
options.B: Alcohol crosses the placenta freely and can cause irreversible fetal brain and physical damage
options.C: Pregnant women possess an allergy that instantly destroys liver cells upon contact
options.D: The fetus metabolizes alcohol three times faster than an adult human

explanation: Alcohol easily passes right through the placenta to the baby. Because it acts as a toxin to developing organs, total abstinence is the safest rule. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T013#GNS227_U4_T013_h5)

question: A patient on a long-term central nervous system depressant asks if they can have a glass of wine with dinner. What should you say?

options.A: Drinking one small glass of wine will help the medication absorb faster into your bloodstream
options.B: Alcohol only interacts negatively with antibiotics, not with nervous system medications
options.C: You must avoid alcohol entirely because combining it with your medication can cause dangerous respiratory depression
options.D: You can safely drink alcohol as long as you take your medication two hours beforehand

explanation: Mixing alcohol with depressants is super dangerous! It can slow breathing down to critical levels, lead to deep comas, or even be fatal. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T013#GNS227_U4_T013_h5)

question: What does the letter 'C' stand for in the popular CAGE alcohol screening tool?

options.A: Craving
options.B: Control
options.C: Chronic
options.D: Cut down

explanation: The 'C' stands for asking if the patient has ever felt they ought to Cut down on their drinking. It's a quick, friendly way to start a health chat. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T013#GNS227_U4_T013_h6)

question: During an assessment, a patient answers 'yes' to three out of four CAGE questions. What is your best next step as a nurse?

options.A: Tell the patient that drinking is completely normal and requires no action
options.B: Perform a detailed follow-up assessment regarding alcohol use patterns and dependence risks
options.C: Ignore the screening results since CAGE is only meant for research purposes
options.D: Immediately discharge the patient without discussing lifestyle habits

explanation: A high CAGE score is a red flag for possible alcohol dependence. It's time to gently dig deeper and offer supportive guidance. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T013#GNS227_U4_T013_h6)

question: Why do scolding or confrontational approaches usually fail when counseling patients about drinking?

options.A: They cause the liver to metabolize alcohol at an unsafe, accelerated speed
options.B: They instantly cure the physiological addiction without patient consent
options.C: They make patients defensive and less likely to share honest information
options.D: They violate federal privacy laws regarding nutritional counseling

explanation: Nobody likes being judged! If a nurse is harsh, the patient will just shut down, hide their habits, and miss out on real help. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T013#GNS227_U4_T013_h7)

question: Which of these is a helpful harm-reduction tip for a patient who chooses to drink alcohol?

options.A: Eating a substantial meal before drinking to help slow down alcohol absorption
options.B: Driving home immediately after finishing the last drink to test reflexes
options.C: Replacing all water intake with high-strength spirits to build immunity
options.D: Consuming alcohol exclusively on an empty stomach to speed up digestion

explanation: Food in the tummy slows down how fast alcohol gets into the bloodstream, helping prevent a sudden, overwhelming spike in drunkenness. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T013#GNS227_U4_T013_h7)

question: What is the main goal of planning a personal diet for a patient?

options.A: Reducing hospital food costs for the facility
options.B: Turning nutritional science into daily food choices
options.C: Eliminating all carbohydrates from the diet
options.D: Ensuring every patient eats the exact same calories

explanation: You're doing great! Diet planning simply takes nutrition rules from the textbook and translates them into the actual meals a person enjoys every day. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T014#GNS227_U4_T014_h1)

question: Why can't nurses just use one standard diet plan for every single patient?

options.A: Because physical, metabolic, and lifestyle needs vary greatly among people
options.B: Because doctors legally cannot approve identical diets for two patients
options.C: Because food guides require a different plan for every day of the year
options.D: Because standard hospital menus never contain enough protein

explanation: Spot on! Every patient has a unique body, age, and lifestyle, so their meal plan needs to match who they are. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T014#GNS227_U4_T014_h1)

question: In nutrition, what does the term DRI stand for?

options.A: Dietary Restriction Index
options.B: Daily Recommended Instructions
options.C: Dietary Reference Intakes
options.D: Daily Routine Intake

explanation: DRIs are just the standard reference values health workers use to check if someone is getting enough nutrients. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T014#GNS227_U4_T014_h2)

question: What is the main job of the Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL)?

options.A: To show the minimum amount of food needed to avoid fatigue
options.B: To determine the cheapest food sources of essential vitamins
options.C: To warn against taking dangerously high amounts of a nutrient
options.D: To calculate the exact number of calories burned during rest

explanation: Think of the UL as a safety warning light. It tells us the highest amount of a nutrient a person can take before it starts causing harm, especially from supplements. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T014#GNS227_U4_T014_h2)

question: Which of these is a classic example of an anthropometric measurement?

options.A: Daily water consumption
options.B: Body mass index
options.C: Serum albumin level
options.D: Blood pressure reading

explanation: You've got this! Anthropometric just means measuring physical body dimensions like height, weight, and BMI. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T014#GNS227_U4_T014_h3)

question: You notice a patient has dry, brittle hair, pale skin, and spoon-shaped nails. What part of the nutritional assessment is this?

options.A: Dietary history recall
options.B: Clinical observations
options.C: Biochemical tests
options.D: Anthropometric tracking

explanation: When you look directly at the patient's body for physical signs of nutrition issues, you are doing a clinical observation! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T014#GNS227_U4_T014_h3)

question: Why do we use visual food guides, like the healthy eating plate?

options.A: To replace the need for professional medical consultations
options.B: To promote expensive imported food items over local produce
options.C: To help clients build balanced meals easily without complex math
options.D: To guarantee that every person loses weight within one week

explanation: Pictures make nutrition easy! Visual guides help patients build healthy meals at a glance without stressing over numbers. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T014#GNS227_U4_T014_h4)

question: According to the healthy plate method, what portion of a meal should be fruits and vegetables?

options.A: The entire plate
options.B: One-quarter
options.C: Three-quarters
options.D: One-half

explanation: Filling half the plate with colorful fruits and veggies is a quick, easy rule to make sure a meal is full of fiber and vitamins. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T014#GNS227_U4_T014_h4)

question: Why is it important to respect a patient's cultural background when planning their meals?

options.A: Because medical science proves cultural foods are superior
options.B: To prevent the client from ever eating carbohydrates
options.C: Because hospital policy strictly forbids serving foreign foods
options.D: To ensure the client is willing and able to follow the meal plan long-term

explanation: People eat what they love! When we respect cultural food preferences, patients are much more likely to stick to their diet. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T014#GNS227_U4_T014_h5)

question: A patient cannot afford expensive imported foods listed on a standard diet sheet. What should you do as their nurse?

options.A: Tell them to stop worrying about nutrition and just eat less food
options.B: Discharge the patient without any dietary plan
options.C: Suggest nutritious, affordable, and culturally familiar local food alternatives
options.D: Insist that they find extra money to buy the prescribed imported items

explanation: Great nursing judgment! Always adapt care to fit the patient's pocket by recommending budget-friendly, local Nigerian food options. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T014#GNS227_U4_T014_h5)

question: What simple hand guide can a patient use to estimate a single portion of meat or protein?

options.A: The back of the wrist
options.B: The tip of the finger
options.C: The palm of the hand
options.D: The entire forearm

explanation: Your hand is always with you! Using the palm is a handy, quick trick for patients to gauge a normal protein serving. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T014#GNS227_U4_T014_h6)

question: What usually happens when someone skips meals all day and eats one massive meal at night?

options.A: Blood sugar spikes and digestive strain
options.B: Lower nighttime blood pressure
options.C: Faster weight loss and improved metabolism
options.D: Better absorption of essential vitamins

explanation: Good to know! Overloading the stomach all at once confuses digestion and causes sudden jumps and crashes in blood sugar. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T014#GNS227_U4_T014_h6)

question: Why do nurses need to review and update diet plans from time to time?

options.A: Because patients get bored eating the same foods for more than three days
options.B: Because hospital regulations require rewriting charts weekly
options.C: Because food items change their vitamin content every single month
options.D: Because client needs, health status, and life circumstances change over time

explanation: Life isn't static, and neither is health! Regular checks ensure the diet plan keeps up with the patient's changing body and life. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T014#GNS227_U4_T014_h7)

question: A client on a weight-loss diet says they are always hungry and haven't lost any weight after four weeks. What should you do?

options.A: Tell the client to stop eating all solid food until the next appointment
options.B: Discharge the client from care for failing to lose weight
options.C: Review the current food intake and adjust the plan collaboratively with the client
options.D: Ignore the feedback because four weeks is not enough time to evaluate

explanation: Teamwork makes the dream work! Sit down with the patient, figure out what's blocking progress together, and tweak the plan so it actually works for them. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T014#GNS227_U4_T014_h7)

question: What is the primary function of carbohydrates in the human body?

options.A: Providing primary energy for daily activities
options.B: Producing essential hormones for growth
options.C: Regulating body temperature through sweating
options.D: Repairing damaged muscle tissues and organs

explanation: Carbohydrates are broken down into glucose, which serves as the body's main and most efficient energy source. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T015#GNS227_U4_T015_h1)

question: Why is including a wide variety of foods in family meal planning so important?

options.A: It guarantees that every family member eats the exact same calorie count
options.B: It prevents nutrient gaps and avoids excessive intake of any single substance
options.C: It ensures the household spends the maximum possible food budget
options.D: It eliminates the need to provide clean drinking water at meals

explanation: Eating a diverse mix of foods makes it far more likely the body gets all necessary vitamins without relying too heavily on one food type. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T015#GNS227_U4_T015_h1)

question: Which nutrient is especially critical for adolescent girls and boys during major growth spurts to support expanding blood volume?

options.A: Vitamin C
options.B: Sodium
options.C: Fiber
options.D: Iron

explanation: Iron is a core component of hemoglobin, which carries oxygen in the blood, making it vital during rapid adolescent growth. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T015#GNS227_U4_T015_h2)

question: A seventy-year-old patient is losing muscle mass and experiencing bone weakness. Which adjustment is most important to emphasize in their daily meal plan?

options.A: Strict reduction of all dietary fats and oils
options.B: Significantly increased total daily caloric intake
options.C: Elimination of all complex carbohydrates
options.D: Higher amounts of protein, vitamin D, and calcium

explanation: Older adults need adequate protein to fight muscle loss and calcium with vitamin D to maintain bone strength despite lower overall calorie needs. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T015#GNS227_U4_T015_h2)

question: How does buying fruits and vegetables in their natural season help a household manage its food budget?

options.A: Purchasing seasonal items prevents the need to cook meals
options.B: In-season produce is typically more abundant and therefore cheaper
options.C: Out-of-season crops always contain more vitamins
options.D: Seasonal foods require chemical preservatives to stay fresh

explanation: High local supply during harvest seasons drives down the cost of fruits and vegetables while maintaining high nutritional quality. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T015#GNS227_U4_T015_h3)

question: Which of the following is an effective strategy for reducing household expenditure on proteins without sacrificing nutrition?

options.A: Buying imported specialty protein powders instead of whole foods
options.B: Purchasing single-serving pre-packaged meals from restaurants
options.C: Removing all forms of protein entirely from the family diet
options.D: Replacing expensive meat cuts with plant-based options like beans and lentils

explanation: Plant proteins offer high nutritional value at a fraction of the cost of red meat or poultry. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T015#GNS227_U4_T015_h3)

question: What is the first practical step a person should take when starting a weekly meal plan?

options.A: Visiting the local market without a list
options.B: Throwing away all existing canned goods
options.C: Ordering takeout food for the upcoming weekend
options.D: Checking current pantry and refrigerator inventory

explanation: Checking what is already at home prevents buying duplicate items and helps build meals around existing ingredients. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T015#GNS227_U4_T015_h4)

question: Why is batch cooking recommended as part of a family meal strategy?

options.A: It permanently eliminates the need to store food in a refrigerator
options.B: It ensures that all food cooked is consumed in one sitting
options.C: It provides quick, healthy meals for busy days and reduces reliance on fast food
options.D: It allows the cook to avoid washing dishes for an entire month

explanation: Preparing larger portions ahead of time saves valuable time on hectic days and prevents impulsive, less nutritious food choices. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T015#GNS227_U4_T015_h4)

question: What is the main reason for using separate cutting boards for raw meat and fresh vegetables?

options.A: Complying with modern kitchen aesthetic trends
options.B: Ensuring that the wooden boards dry out faster
options.C: Preventing cross-contamination of harmful bacteria
options.D: Keeping the vegetable board from smelling like spices

explanation: Using separate boards stops bacteria from raw meat from transferring to foods that will be eaten raw or lightly cooked. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T015#GNS227_U4_T015_h5)

question: Which cooking method is best for preserving water-soluble vitamins in vegetables?

options.A: Boiling in a large pot for an hour
options.B: Soaking in cold water overnight
options.C: Steaming or quick stir-frying
options.D: Frying deeply in reused cooking oil

explanation: Steaming uses minimal water and short exposure times, preventing valuable vitamins from leaking out into cooking water. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T015#GNS227_U4_T015_h5)

question: What is the best way to handle a young child who refuses to eat a newly introduced vegetable?

options.A: Offer it repeatedly over time alongside familiar foods without forcing them
options.B: Punish the child by sending them away from the dinner table immediately
options.C: Stop offering all vegetables permanently to avoid any further stress
options.D: Force the child to finish every single bite on the plate before sleeping

explanation: Children often need multiple exposures to a new food before accepting it, and pressure only increases mealtime anxiety. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T015#GNS227_U4_T015_h6)

question: A family member has newly diagnosed hypertension and requires a low-salt diet. What is the most practical nursing advice for the household cook?

options.A: Prepare two completely different meals every single day for every person
options.B: Stop cooking altogether and buy canned processed foods for everyone
options.C: Add extra salt to the main pot and give the patient plain water
options.D: Cook the base meal with minimal salt and let others add salt at the table

explanation: This approach keeps cooking manageable for the household while protecting the health of the family member with hypertension. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T015#GNS227_U4_T015_h6)

question: What is the primary goal of performing a nutritional assessment on a patient?

options.A: To catch nutritional problems early and plan care
options.B: To calculate the exact daily financial food budget
options.C: To determine the patient's favorite childhood meals
options.D: To test for rare genetic blood disorders

explanation: Nutritional assessments are designed to spot imbalances early so nurses and doctors can intervene before healing is delayed. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h1)

question: Why must a nurse look at more than just a patient's current weight during a nutritional evaluation?

options.A: Hospital scales are frequently broken and unreliable
options.B: Patients often lie about their true weight
options.C: Weight alone does not reveal hidden nutrient deficiencies or tissue changes
options.D: Weight changes only matter after discharge

explanation: A complete evaluation combines dietary, biochemical, and physical data because weight fluctuations can mean many things. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h1)

question: What does the letter 'B' stand for in the ABCD approach to nutritional assessment?

options.A: Body mass index
options.B: Biochemical data
options.C: Bowel movements
options.D: Baseline weight

explanation: In the ABCD framework, B stands for biochemical, which refers to laboratory tests and blood work. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h2)

question: A nurse checks a patient's skin, hair, and oral mucosa for signs of vitamin deficiencies. Which part of the ABCD framework is this?

options.A: Dietary history
options.B: Anthropometric measurements
options.C: Clinical examination
options.D: Biochemical data

explanation: Looking directly at physical features like hair texture and mucous membranes falls under the clinical examination category. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h2)

question: Which factor is a major warning sign for nutritional risk in hospitalized patients?

options.A: Involuntary weight loss
options.B: Sleeping on the left side
options.C: Preferring sweet drinks
options.D: Wearing loose clothing

explanation: Unplanned or involuntary weight loss is one of the strongest indicators that a patient is at high risk for malnutrition. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h3)

question: Why can an overweight patient still suffer from malnutrition?

options.A: Excess body fat does not guarantee adequate vitamin and protein intake
options.B: Overweight patients are unable to absorb any nutrients
options.C: Lab tests cannot measure nutrition in larger bodies
options.D: Obesity completely stops the digestive tract from working

explanation: Malnutrition means poor nutrition, which includes lacking essential vitamins and minerals regardless of body weight. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h3)

question: When should nutritional screening typically happen for a newly admitted hospital patient?

options.A: Right before the patient is discharged home
options.B: At the final weekly multidisciplinary meeting
options.C: Only after the patient requests a meal tray
options.D: Within twenty-four hours of admission

explanation: Early screening within the first day helps catch risks before the patient's condition deteriorates. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h4)

question: What is the main difference between nutritional screening and a full nutritional assessment?

options.A: Screening is done by doctors, while assessment is done by cooks
options.B: Screening is only used for children, while assessment is for adults
options.C: Screening is a quick check to find risk, while assessment is a deep dive
options.D: Screening only looks at lab work, while assessment only looks at weight

explanation: Screening quickly identifies who is at risk, prompting a thorough assessment to diagnose specific nutritional problems. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h4)

question: How does untreated malnutrition directly affect a patient's recovery in the hospital?

options.A: It causes immediate memory loss in older adults
options.B: It lowers blood pressure to dangerous levels instantly
options.C: It delays wound healing and increases infection risk
options.D: It stops intravenous medications from working entirely

explanation: Without proper nutrients, the body lacks the building blocks needed to repair tissue and fight off hospital germs. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h5)

question: Which of the following complications is strongly linked to poor nutritional status in bedridden patients?

options.A: Ear infections
options.B: Kidney stones
options.C: Vision loss
options.D: Pressure injuries

explanation: Malnourished tissue breaks down much faster under pressure, making pressure injuries very common in vulnerable patients. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h5)

question: What is the main purpose of taking a nutrition history in nursing practice?

options.A: To gather information about a patient's food intake and eating habits
options.B: To strictly calculate the exact daily financial cost of groceries
options.C: To diagnose rare genetic metabolic disorders immediately
options.D: To prescribe specific medical diets without consulting a doctor

explanation: A nutrition history focuses directly on understanding what and how a patient eats to guide their care. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h1)

question: Why is a nutrition history considered a vital part of a standard patient admission assessment?

options.A: It helps catch early warning signs of poor nourishment before severe illness develops
options.B: It replaces the need to check vital signs or physical examination findings
options.C: It ensures the hospital kitchen meets local food safety inspection standards
options.D: It guarantees that the patient will never experience any weight loss

explanation: Early identification of dietary issues allows nurses to intervene before nutritional problems turn into major health complications. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h1)

question: What is the primary goal of a dietary assessment?

options.A: To determine the exact brand of food the patient prefers to buy
options.B: To evaluate nutritional status and check for adequate nutrient intake
options.C: To calculate the patient's daily physical exercise routine accurately
options.D: To test for food allergies using a series of skin prick procedures

explanation: Evaluating whether a patient gets enough essential nutrients is the central objective of any dietary assessment. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h2)

question: A nurse uses a dietary assessment to establish a baseline. What does this mean for patient care?

options.A: It provides a starting point to measure future nutritional changes and treatment progress
options.B: It acts as a permanent record that cannot be altered during the hospital stay
options.C: It proves that the patient has no underlying metabolic diseases
options.D: It serves as the final clearance for the patient to be discharged home

explanation: Establishing a baseline gives healthcare providers a reference point to see if interventions are helping or if the patient's condition is worsening. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h2)

question: Which of the following is included in a comprehensive nutrition history?

options.A: Family tree and genetic ancestry
options.B: Medical history and medication use
options.C: Recent travel history outside the country
options.D: Workplace safety hazard inspections

explanation: Medical conditions and medications heavily influence how the body absorbs and uses nutrients, making them essential parts of a nutrition history. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h3)

question: A patient takes a daily diuretic medication that causes frequent urination. Why must a nurse note this during a nutrition history?

options.A: Medications have no bearing on nutritional status and can be ignored
options.B: Patients on diuretics are legally prohibited from eating high-protein foods
options.C: Diuretics completely replace the need for dietary fiber in older adults
options.D: Certain medications can affect nutrient levels and fluid balance in the body

explanation: Many drugs interact with nutrients, alter appetite, or cause losses of vitamins and minerals, which a nurse must account for. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h3)

question: What is the main limitation of using a 24-hour dietary recall?

options.A: It relies heavily on the patient's memory and may not show normal eating habits
options.B: It is too expensive for routine use in busy outpatient clinics
options.C: It requires the patient to write down every meal for an entire month
options.D: It only measures fluid intake and ignores solid foods entirely
